questions.explanation: 1100 AND 1010 = 1000 = 8. AND sets a bit only when both inputs have it.

questions.prompt: What is `12 ^ 10`?
questions.explanation: 1100 XOR 1010 = 0110 = 6. XOR sets a bit when exactly one input has it Ã¢â‚¬â€ note the last row of the table, where both having it cancels out.

questions.prompt: How do you test whether bit 5 of a flags variable is set?
options: if (flags == (1 << 5))
if (flags & (1u << 5))
if (flags || (1 << 5))
if (~flags & (1 << 5))
questions.explanation: AND with a mask containing only that bit. Use `&&` for the boolean test and 1u so the shift is unsigned and stays in range.

questions.prompt: What is the value of `~0` when x is an unsigned int?
options: The maximum value of the type, e.g. 4294967295 for 32-bit unsigned
Undefined behaviour
questions.explanation: ~ flips every bit, so all zeros become all ones. The result depends on the width of the type, which is why the answer is stated as "the maximum value of the type" rather than a number.

questions.prompt: Why is `1 << 31` undefined behaviour but `1u << 31` is not?
options: They are identical
1 is a signed int and cannot be shifted into the sign bit; 1u is unsigned so the bit is just another bit
Unsigned shifts are always safe
31 is too large a shift count
questions.explanation: Left-shifting a positive signed value so that the result is not representable in the signed type is undefined. With an unsigned left operand the same shift is well-defined, which is why masks are written 1u << n.

questions.prompt: What does `a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b;` do?
options: Adds b to a twice
Swaps a and b without a temporary Ã¢â‚¬â€ but only reliably for integers
Zeros both variables
Nothing useful
questions.explanation: It is the XOR swap: a^=b puts a^b in a, b^=a recovers the original a, a^=b swaps them. It is not guaranteed for floating point and a plain temporary is clearer, so real code should use one.

lessons.title: Precedence and associativity
lessons.summary: The full table, the rules that generate the bugs, and when to just use more parentheses.

payload.text:
## Precedence decides which operator binds first

In `2 + 3 * 4`, `*` binds tighter than `+`, so it is `2 + (3 * 4) = 14`, not `(2 + 3) * 4 = 20`.

## The table, from tightest to loosest binding

Read this top to bottom; earlier rows bind tighter.

| Level | Operators | Associativity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `()` `[]` `->` `.` `++` `--` (postfix) | left to right |
| 2 | `!` `~` `+` `-` (prefix) `++` `--` (prefix) `&` `*` `sizeof` `_Alignof` | right to left |
| 3 | `*` `/` `%` | left to right |
| 4 | `+` `-` | left to right |
| 5 | `<<` `>>` | left to right |
| 6 | `<` `<=` `>` `>=` | left to right |
| 7 | `==` `!=` | left to right |
| 8 | `&` | left to right |
| 9 | `^` | left to right |
| 10 | `|` | left to right |
| 11 | `&&` | left to right |
| 12 | `||` | left to right |
| 13 | `?` `:` | right to left |
| 14 | `=` `*=` `/=` `%=` `+=` `-=` `<<=` `>>=` `&=` `^=` `|=` | right to left |
| 15 | `,` | left to right |

## Four rules that produce almost all the bugs

**1. `=` has very low precedence.** It binds *looser* than almost everything.

```c
if (x = y + 1)      /* parses as if (x = (y + 1)) */
```

**2. `&` binds looser than `==`.** This surprises people coming from languages where it is the reverse.

```c
if (a & b == 0)     /* WRONG: parses as a & (b == 0).
                       The comparison runs first, producing 0 or 1,
                       and then the whole condition is 0 or 1 Ã¢â‚¬â€ the bitwise
                       AND is not testing what you thought. */
if ((a & b) == 0)   /* correct */
```

**3. Relational (<, >) binds tighter than equality (==, !=).**

```c
a < b == c < d     /* parses as ((a < b) == (c < d)) */
```

Usually harmless, but it is a genuine surprise when reading code you did not write.

**4. `->` and `.` are the tightest thing there is.**

```c
(*p).field          /* correct: dereference, then take a member */
*p.field            /* WRONG: parses as *(p.field), which needs p to be
                       a pointer to a struct that itself has a pointer
                       member named field. Usually a compile error. */
```

## The rule that settles everything

> **If you are not certain, add parentheses.**

There is no prize for writing dense expressions. C code is read far more often than it is written, and an expression with explicit parentheses costs nothing at runtime Ã¢â‚¬â€ the compiler does not care.

```c
/* ugly */
if (x = f(a) + b * c) { ... }

/* obvious */
total = f(a) + (b * c);
if (total != 0) { ... }
```

The second version is not "for beginners". It is what experienced C programmers write.

## The comma operator

```c
for (int i = 0, j = n - 1; i < j; i++, j--) { ... }
```

The comma operator evaluates the left operand, discards its value, then evaluates the right. It is a sequencing point. It exists mostly to let `for` headers and macro bodies hold several expressions. Outside those two places, use a semicolon Ã¢â‚¬â€ the comma operator is nearly always a mistake.

## Sequencing and undefined behaviour

Between two **sequence points**, you may modify a variable at most once, and you may not both modify and read it. Anything else is undefined behaviour.

C99 removed most sequence points; C11 restored the concept as *sequenced before* and *sequenced after*, which is more precise. The practical rule has not changed:

```c
int i = 0;
int a = i++ + ++i;    /* UB: i modified twice with no sequencing */
int b = (i++, i);     /* fine: the comma operator sequences them */
int c = i ? i++ : 0;  /* UB: i modified and read in the same expression */
```

`printf("%d %d\n", i++, i++)` is the famous one. It "works" on some compilers at some optimisation levels and produces a different answer after you change the compiler version. Never do it.
### The mistakes this table prevents

payload.title: Precedence traps
rows: same Ã¢â‚¬â€ this one is fine
a < b && a == c Ã¢â‚¬â€ the intent is unclear
same Ã¢â‚¬â€ the order is as written

payload.title: What `-Wall` catches for you
payload.text: GCC and Clang both warn on `a & b == 0` with -Wparentheses ("suggest parentheses around arithmetic in operand of &"), and on `x = y` inside a condition with -Wparentheses as well. Turning on -Wparentheses is a cheap way to have the compiler audit your precedence assumptions.

payload.title: Do not try to be clever with precedence
payload.text: Every hour spent mentally parsing a dense C expression is an hour better spent putting parentheses in. Compilers do not reward density, reviewers punish it, and the -Wparentheses warnings will find the dangerous cases for free.

questions.prompt: In C, how does `a & b == 0` parse?
options: It is a syntax error
questions.explanation: Equality binds tighter than bitwise AND. The comparison runs first producing 0 or 1, and the AND then does almost nothing useful. Write (a & b) == 0.

questions.prompt: What is the value of `2 + 3 * 4` and `2 * 3 + 4`?
options: 20 and 20
14 and 10
14 and 14
20 and 14
questions.explanation: Multiplication binds tighter than addition, so these are 2 + (3*4) = 14 and (2*3) + 4 = 10.

questions.prompt: How do you correctly access a member through a pointer to a struct?
options: p.field
(*p).field
*p.field
p->field only
questions.explanation: (*p).field dereferences then accesses. p->field is a shorthand for exactly that and is preferred. *p.field is the wrong parse: it is *(p.field).

questions.prompt: Why is `printf("%d %d", i++, i++)` undefined behaviour?
options: printf does not support two arguments
i is modified twice in one expression with no sequencing between the modifications
++ does not work on int
The format string is wrong
questions.explanation: Between sequence points you may modify a variable at most once. Two modifications of i in a single argument list violates that, and -Wall reports it.

questions.prompt: Which operator has the lowest precedence of those listed?
questions.explanation: Assignment binds looser than arithmetic, relational and equality operators, which is why `if (x = y + 1)` assigns y+1 to x.

modules.title: Module 6 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Control Flow
modules.summary: Choosing, repeating, and the specific ways C control flow betrays you.

lessons.title: if, else, and the conditions that are never true
lessons.summary: if/else chains, the dangling else, and four ways a condition silently evaluates wrong.

payload.title: The braces rule, stated once
payload.text: Use braces for every if, every for, every while, every function body. No exceptions, no style debates. A one-line if that later grows a second line is the single most common source of a silently-wrong nested conditional in C, and braces cost nothing.

payload.title: A signed result stored in an unsigned variable
payload.text: `size_t` and `unsigned int` results compared with `< 0` never enter the branch. This is not theoretical: it is how buffer-handling code ends up proceeding with a failed read, and it is found in real production systems regularly. Check the return value against the type you actually have.

questions.prompt: In `if (x = 5)`, what happens?
options: The condition tests whether x is 5
5 is assigned to x, and the condition is true because 5 is non-zero
It is a compile error
The condition is false because assignments cannot be conditions
questions.explanation: Assignment is an expression whose value is the assigned value. 5 is non-zero so the body runs, and x is now 5. -Wall warns about exactly this.

questions.prompt: What does the `else` in `if (a) if (b) x=1; else x=2;` attach to?
options: The outer if
The inner if, the nearest unmatched one
It is a syntax error
Neither Ã¢â‚¬â€ the else is required to match the outer if
questions.explanation: C attaches else to the closest unmatched if. The braces you need to change the meaning must go around the outer if. -Wdangling-else warns about this.

questions.prompt: Why is `if (bytes_read < 0)` dead code when bytes_read is unsigned?
options: Because < 0 is not allowed on unsigned types
Because bytes_read is converted to unsigned, and no unsigned value is less than zero
Because the compiler optimises it away
Because it should be <= 0
questions.explanation: The comparison converts 0 to unsigned, and no unsigned value is negative, so the branch is unreachable. This pattern disables real error checks and is a known security bug shape.

questions.prompt: What is the value of the condition `ptr` where ptr is a valid non-NULL pointer?
options: ptr itself, and it is true because it is non-zero
The address, which is true because addresses are non-zero
The value ptr points to
questions.explanation: A pointer used directly as a condition is true if it is not null. This is why `if (ptr)` is the idiomatic null check.

questions.prompt: What is the value of `3 > 1 > 2` in C?
options: It is a syntax error
0, because (3 > 1) is 1, and 1 > 2 is false
1, because 3 is greater than 1 which is greater than 2
It is a compile error in C11 and later
questions.explanation: Comparison yields 0 or 1, and the second comparison then compares that 1 against 2. C has no chained comparison operator.

lessons.title: switch: cases, break, fallthrough, and default
lessons.summary: How switch really works, why break matters, and when fallthrough is a feature.

payload.title: switch rules at a glance
rows: The controlling value is an integer
int, char, enum Ã¢â‚¬â€ not float or double
switch(d) with a double is an error
Execution continues into the next case
Forgetting break is the classic bug
case 1: case 2: body Ã¢â‚¬â€ legal and idiomatic
A declaration in one case is visible in all
Nothing runs if nothing matches and there is no default
Inside a loop, break leaves the loop

payload.title: Making fallthrough explicit is worth the keystrokes
payload.text: If two cases genuinely share behaviour, group them with empty labels rather than by omitting break. If execution should genuinely continue from one case into the next, write a `/* fall through */` comment and compile with -Wimplicit-fallthrough so the compiler agrees with your intent instead of guessing.

payload.title: DuffÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s device
payload.text: C permits a `case` label inside a loop, letting the loop be entered at an arbitrary case Ã¢â‚¬â€ this is legal, was written by a very good programmer, and is a famous example of C being more powerful than it should be. You will see it in old code. Do not write it, and do not be surprised by it.

questions.prompt: What happens if a `case` has no `break`?
options: The switch stops at the end of the case
Execution continues into the next case, executing its statements too
It is a compile error
The switch restarts from the top
questions.explanation: switch is a jump followed by ordinary sequential execution. There is no implicit end to a case, so statements fall through until a break.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a legal case label?
options: a variable holding a value read at runtime
an enumeration constant
a function call
a floating point literal
questions.explanation: Case labels must be compile-time integer constant expressions. Enum constants, integer literals and character literals qualify; a runtime variable or a function call does not.

questions.prompt: Why is `switch (some_double)` a compile error?
options: Because doubles are too large
Because switch works only on integer types
Because doubles need %f
It is legal, just slow
questions.explanation: The controlling expression must have integer type. To branch on a real number you need an if/else chain, and you should also remember that == on doubles is usually the wrong test anyway.

questions.prompt: You declare `int x = 5;` inside `case 1:` without braces. What is the problem?
options: Nothing
The switch body is a single block, so x is also in scope in every other case, where it would be uninitialised
C does not allow declarations in a switch
x would shadow mainÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s x
questions.explanation: All cases share one block. Wrapping each case in { } gives it its own scope, which is almost always what you want.

questions.prompt: What does an empty `case 2:` label followed by `case 3:` achieve?
options: A syntax error
The two values share one body, so 2 and 3 run the same code
2 is ignored
The switch falls through to default
questions.explanation: An empty label is a legal no-op that groups values, so both 2 and 3 execute the same statements. This is the standard way to write a multi-value case.

lessons.title: while, for, and do-while
lessons.summary: The three loop forms, the three-part for header, and how to write a loop that terminates.

payload.title: A for loop, one statement at a time

steps.caption: sum is initialised to 0. The for header is about to run its first part.
Part 1 of the header: int i = 1. This runs exactly once, before the loop.
Part 2: the condition i <= 5 is 1 <= 5, which is true. Enter the body.
Body: sum += i, so sum becomes 0 + 1 = 1.
Part 3: i++ makes i 2. Then the condition is tested again: 2 <= 5, true.
steps.note: Note the order: update first, THEN test. This is why a continue in the body still runs i++ Ã¢â‚¬â€ it jumps to part 3, not part 2.

steps.caption: Body again: sum = 1 + 2 = 3.
i becomes 3, then 4, then 5. sum climbs: 6, 10, 15.
i becomes 6. Now 6 <= 5 is false, so the loop exits and the body does not run again.
steps.note: The loop ran for i = 1,2,3,4,5 Ã¢â‚¬â€ five iterations for five values, because the condition used <=. Had it used <, it would have stopped at i = 5 and sum would be 10.

steps.caption: The statement after the loop runs: sum = 15.

payload.text: ### Choosing the right loop

payload.title: Which loop for which job
rows: The count is the point; keep the three parts together
Repeat until a sentinel value is read
There is no count, only a condition
Prompt for input at least once
The body must run before the first test
The termination condition is the data itself
Same idea, tested through the value
And make sure the bound is the array size, not a literal

payload.title: The loop that never overflows
payload.text: When in doubt about an unsigned index, use `size_t` and `< array_length`. `for (size_t i = 0; i < count; i++)` with `count` a `size_t` cannot underflow, and the type matches what the array length functions return.

payload.title: continue in a while loop can hang the program
payload.text: In a for loop, continue jumps to the update so the counter still advances. In a while loop, continue jumps back to the condition Ã¢â‚¬â€ so if the counter update was the last line of the body, `continue` above it skips it and the loop spins forever. Put the increment at the top, or use a for loop.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `for` and `while`?
options: for is faster
None in what they do Ã¢â‚¬â€ a for loop is exactly the equivalent initialise/test/update plus a while. Use for when the loop is counted.
while cannot contain break
for can only loop over arrays
questions.explanation: They are the same statement in different clothes. The for form exists so the three parts of a counted loop sit together on one line.

questions.prompt: What does `continue` do inside a for loop?
options: Jumps to the condition test
Skips the rest of the body and runs the update expression, then tests again
Exits the loop
Restarts the loop from the beginning with i reset to 0
questions.explanation: continue jumps to the update expression in a for loop. In a while loop it jumps to the condition, which is why `continue` can cause an infinite loop there.

questions.prompt: Why is `unsigned int n = 10; while (n > 0) { n = n - 1; }` safe but `while (n--)` confusing?
options: Both are identical
The first never decrements from 0 because the test fails first; the second leaves n at UINT_MAX when the loop ends
The second never terminates
n - 1 is not allowed on unsigned
questions.explanation: Both terminate, but n-- leaves n as UINT_MAX at the end because the post-decrement test is evaluated with the pre-decrement value. Never use n after such a loop.

questions.prompt: How many times does `for (int i = 0; i <= 5; i++)` execute its body?
options: 4 times
5 times
6 times
5 or 6 depending on the starting value
questions.explanation: i takes the values 0,1,2,3,4,5 Ã¢â‚¬â€ six iterations. If you meant 0 through 4 you should have written i < 5.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with `while (j < 5) { if (j == 3) continue; j++; }`?
options: Nothing
When j is 3, continue skips the j++, so j stays 3 forever and the loop never ends
continue is not allowed in a while loop
j is uninitialised
questions.explanation: continue in a while loop jumps to the condition, and the only statement that changes j is after it. This is why the counter update belongs at the top of the body, or in a for loop.

questions.prompt: Why must a loop over a linked list check `n != NULL` in the header rather than the body?
options: Style preference only
Because an empty list has head == NULL, and the body would dereference it on the first iteration before reaching any check
Because NULL cannot be compared in a body
It makes no difference
questions.explanation: The test is the loop condition. A do-while with the check in the body is the exact shape of this bug.

modules.title: Module 7 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Functions
modules.summary: Decomposition, prototypes, pass by value, scope, recursion, and function pointers.

lessons.title: Declaring and defining: the rule that trips everyone up
lessons.summary: Why C needs prototypes, the order rule, and what actually happens when you call a function before defining it.

payload.title: Compile with -Wmissing-prototypes
payload.text: It warns when a non-static function has no prototype visible. That catches typos in function names and missing declarations in exactly the situations where the compiler would otherwise assume the wrong signature.

payload.title: The declaration and the definition must match exactly
payload.text: If your header says `int process(char *buf, size_t n);` and the .c file says `int process(const char *buf, size_t n);`, that is not a warning you can ignore Ã¢â‚¬â€ they are different functions as far as the linker is concerned, and you get "undefined reference". Type them once in the header and never retype the signature.

questions.prompt: Why must a function be declared before it is used?
options: For documentation only
Because the compiler must know its return type and parameter types in order to check the call and generate correct code
Because the linker cannot handle forward references
It does not have to Ã¢â‚¬â€ modern C figures it out
questions.explanation: The call must type-check and generate the correct machine code, which needs the signature. Before C99 the compiler would assume int, and if that was wrong the caller read the wrong bytes.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a declaration and a definition?
options: A declaration provides the body, a definition does not
A declaration introduces a name and its type; a definition also allocates storage (objects) or provides the body (functions)
They are the same thing in different files
Declarations are only for static functions
questions.explanation: extern marks a declaration, and a declaration in a header is a declaration. Only one definition per object or function may exist across the whole program.

questions.prompt: A non-void function reaches its closing brace without a return. What is that?
options: It returns 0
Undefined behaviour Ã¢â‚¬â€ the caller gets an indeterminate value
A compile-time warning and nothing more
It returns the last expression value
questions.explanation: The function has no defined return value. -Wall reports it as "control reaches end of non-void function". main is the one exception since C99.

questions.prompt: What does `static` mean on a file-scope function?
options: Its value is preserved between calls
Internal linkage: only code in this .c file can call it
It cannot be called from other files, but it is still exported for linking
It is faster
questions.explanation: At file scope, static restricts the name to the current translation unit. The function is private to the file, which lets the compiler inline it freely and prevents collisions.

questions.prompt: You get "undefined reference to process" but process is defined in utils.c. What is wrong?
options: process is misspelled in the definition
utils.o was not compiled or not passed to the linker
The header is missing an include guard
process must be static
questions.explanation: The declaration in the header satisfied the compiler. Only the linker collects definitions, so utils.o must be on the link line: gcc -o app main.c utils.c.

lessons.title: Pass by value: why your callerÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s variable did not change
lessons.summary: The copy, the three ways to get a real change, and the ownership question every pointer parameter must answer.

payload.title: Pass by value vs pass by pointer

steps.caption: The caller has x = 5. On the left, the value is copied in. On the right, the address is copied in.
steps.note: The left function gets a value. The right gets an address it can write through. Everything that follows is a consequence of that one difference.

steps.caption: Inside f, `n = 999;` assigns to the copy. The callerÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s x is a different object in a different place.
steps.note: Two objects, same value, unrelated. This is why the change is lost.

steps.caption: Now the right-hand function does `*p = 999;`. The * dereferences, so it writes to the object the address points at.
steps.note: The pointer p is still a copy Ã¢â‚¬â€ the function still cannot change which address p holds. It can only change what that address points to.

steps.caption: When f returns, the copies are gone. On the left nothing survives. On the right the callerÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s x is 999.

payload.text: ### Choosing the right approach

payload.title: What to pass, and how
rows: To modify which pointer the caller holds
a pointer to the first element, plus the length

payload.title: The const-says-what-you-wont-do rule
payload.text: If your function does not modify what a pointer points to, write `const T *p`. It is a promise to every future caller, it is checked by the compiler on their side, and it often lets the compiler generate better code because it knows the function cannot write through that pointer.

payload.title: sizeof on a parameter is the size of a pointer
payload.text: `void f(int arr[])` receives a pointer, so `sizeof arr` inside f is 8 (or 4) Ã¢â‚¬â€ the size of a pointer, not the array. Every C programmer gets this wrong once. The array only exists in the callerÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s frame. If you need the count, pass it, and take `size_t` rather than `int`.

questions.prompt: In C, arguments are passed...
options: by reference, like C++
by value, always
by value for small types and by reference for large ones
by pointer if they are declared as pointers
questions.explanation: Always by value. Passing a pointer is not a different calling convention; it is passing a value that happens to be an address, which the callee can then dereference.

questions.prompt: Why does `sizeof arr` inside `void f(int arr[])` give 8 rather than the array size?
options: Because sizeof is broken for arrays
Because a parameter declared as an array is actually a pointer parameter Ã¢â‚¬â€ the array decays
Because the function does not know the size
Because arrays are always 8 bytes
questions.explanation: Array parameters are pointer parameters. The function has no idea how many elements there are, which is why you must pass the length.

questions.prompt: What is the correct meaning of `int (*p)[10];`?
options: An array of 10 pointers to int
A pointer to an array of 10 ints
An array of 10 arrays of int
A function taking 10 ints
questions.explanation: Read from the name outward: p is a pointer, to an array, of 10 ints. Without the parentheses, int *p[10] would be an array of 10 pointers.

questions.prompt: Why should a function that only reads a char buffer take `const char *` rather than `char *`?
options: To make it faster
To document that the function will not modify the callerÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s data, and to let the compiler skip aliasing checks
Because char * is deprecated
So that the caller can pass a string literal
questions.explanation: It is a promise the compiler can verify at the call site, it costs nothing, and it lets the optimiser assume the function does not write through that pointer.

questions.prompt: A function returns a mallocÃ¢â‚¬â„¢d buffer. What must the documentation say?
options: Nothing, that is obvious
That the caller owns it and must free() it, and that the function does not free anything it was given
That the buffer is static
That the function also takes ownership of its arguments
questions.explanation: C has no ownership tracking. Every pointer parameter crosses a function boundary carrying an implicit ownership question, and the only mechanism is documentation plus consistent conventions.

lessons.title: Recursion and the call stack
lessons.summary: Base case, the recursive case, what actually happens in memory, and when recursion is the wrong tool.

payload.title: factorial(5), frame by frame

steps.caption: Empty stack. Nothing has been called yet.
main calls factorial(5). A frame is pushed holding the argument and the return address.
steps.note: The return address is what lets the CPU know to come back to main. It is why the stack is LIFO: the last thing pushed is the first thing returned to.

steps.caption: n = 5 is not <= 1, so it calls factorial(4). A second frame is pushed on top.
Three deep. Each frame is a completely separate copy of n Ã¢â‚¬â€ the recursive call gets its own.
steps.note: This is why the function works: the 4 lives in its own frame and is not disturbed while the 5 sits below it. Variables do not overwrite each other because each call has its own storage.

steps.caption: Four and five deep. The base case is next.
n = 1 hits the base case and returns 1. The frame is popped, and 1 is handed back to the caller.
steps.note: A return is a pop plus a value. The frame, its locals and its return address all stop existing Ã¢â‚¬â€ which is why returning a pointer to a local is a dangling pointer.

steps.caption: Unwinding. Each frame returns to its caller, which resumes at the return address stored when it was called.
One frame left. It computes 5 * 24 = 120 and returns to main.
The stack is empty again and main has its answer. Six frames were used at peak depth.
steps.note: Six frames of ~32 bytes is about 200 bytes of stack for a five-deep recursion. Factorially, n = 100000 would use a few megabytes Ã¢â‚¬â€ which is why iterative factorial is preferred in real code.

payload.title: Freeing a tree, in the right order

steps.caption: A three-node tree. root has two children, and the left child has one of its own.
tree_free(root): recurse into root->left first.
Left has no children, so it is freed. It is gone.
steps.note: The recursion returns, and control comes back to the frame for n1.

steps.caption: Now recurse into root->right, then free root itself.
Empty. Every node was freed exactly once.
steps.note: The order matters: free the children BEFORE the parent. If you freed root first and then touched root->left, that is a use-after-free Ã¢â‚¬â€ reading a pointer to memory that has been returned to the allocator.

payload.title: Never return the address of a local
payload.text: A local variable lives in the current stack frame. When the function returns, that frame is reused by the next call. Any pointer you returned to it is now dangling. This is not a rare edge case Ã¢â‚¬â€ it is the single most common way beginners produce a "works until the next function call, then garbage" bug. The compiler can catch it with -Wreturn-local-addr.

payload.title: Use a loop when the data is flat, recursion when it is a tree
payload.text: The test is simple: if the structure has a fixed number of levels and you can say "for each element" in one sentence, use a loop. If the structure contains itself Ã¢â‚¬â€ trees, lists, nested expressions, nested directories Ã¢â‚¬â€ recursion will be shorter and clearer than anything you can write with an explicit stack.

questions.prompt: What is missing from this factorial? int f(int n) { if (n == 0) return 1; return n * f(n - 1); }
options: A semicolon
The base case is unreachable for negative n, so f(0) recurses to f(-1) and underflows forever
It is correct
It needs unsigned, not int
questions.explanation: The recursive case uses n - 1, so the domain includes negatives, and n == 0 is never true for them. `if (n <= 1)` is the correct base case for this shape of function.

questions.prompt: What does each recursive call get in its own copy?
options: Nothing Ã¢â‚¬â€ all frames share the same variables
Its own stack frame with its own copy of the parameters and locals
A single global copy
Nothing; recursion has no memory cost
questions.explanation: Every call pushes a new frame containing its own parameters, locals and return address. That is why the calls do not interfere with each other, and why deep recursion consumes stack.

questions.prompt: Why must you not return the address of a local variable?
options: It is slow
The stack frame is released on return and reused, so the pointer dangles
Locals have no addresses
It only works for static variables
questions.explanation: The frame disappears when the function returns. Any pointer into it is dangling the moment control leaves Ã¢â‚¬â€ the memory may look intact until the next call overwrites it, which is what makes the bug intermittent.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a good reason to use recursion?
options: It is always faster than a loop
The data is itself recursive, such as a tree or a nested expression
It uses less memory
C requires it for some operations
questions.explanation: Recursion matches recursive data. For flat sequences a loop is both clearer and constant-space, and recursion costs stack proportional to depth.

questions.prompt: What is the correct order to free a tree?
options: Free the node, then its children
Free the children recursively, then the node
Free the root, then walk again
It does not matter
questions.explanation: Children first. Freeing the parent first and then reading node->left is a use-after-free, because the parentÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s memory has already been returned to the allocator.

lessons.title: Function pointers and callbacks
lessons.summary: The one place C supports polymorphism, and why it matters for interfaces, dispatch tables and testability.

payload.title: The three real uses of function pointers
payload.text: Callbacks (pass behaviour in), dispatch tables (choose behaviour from data), and vtables (object-oriented C). The first two are everyday. The third is how every C library that pretends to have classes is actually built.

payload.title: Calling through a null or dangling function pointer
payload.text: A function pointer that is NULL jumps to address 0. One that was returned by a function whose frame has gone jumps to freed stack memory. Both are crashes, and both are common enough that "is this pointer valid?" is a question worth asking every time you store one.

questions.prompt: How do you declare a pointer to a function taking two ints and returning int?
options: int *func(int, int);
int (*func)(int, int);
int func*(int, int);
(int*) func(int, int);
questions.explanation: Parentheses around the name make it a pointer to a function. Without them, int *func(int,int) declares a FUNCTION returning a pointer to int.

questions.prompt: What is the point of taking `const void *` parameters in a qsort comparison function?
options: It makes the function faster
It promises the function will not modify the data, and it lets qsort work with any type by casting back
It is required for portability
It avoids the need for a cast
questions.explanation: qsort is generic, so it deals in void*. Your function casts back to the real type. The const documents that comparison does not modify the data.

questions.prompt: Why is a dispatch table of function pointers often better than a switch?
options: It is faster at runtime
Adding an operation means one function and one array row, instead of editing a switch, and the compiler checks the signature
Switches do not work with enums
It uses less memory
questions.explanation: The maintenance win is the point. A switch needs a new case and a new function; a table needs a new function and one row. The compiler also verifies every row has the right signature.

questions.prompt: What happens when you call a function pointer whose value is NULL?
options: It returns 0
It is undefined behaviour Ã¢â‚¬â€ in practice a jump to address 0 and a crash
The compiler inserts a runtime check
It calls a default handler
questions.explanation: There is no runtime check. Always test a function pointer against NULL before calling it.

questions.prompt: What does `(a > b) - (a < b)` produce?
options: A boolean
-1 when a < b, 0 when equal, 1 when a > b
The difference a - b
1 or -1, non-deterministic order
questions.explanation: Both comparisons yield 0 or 1, so subtracting them gives exactly -1, 0 or 1 Ã¢â‚¬â€ the return convention qsort requires.

modules.title: Module 8 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Arrays and strings
modules.summary: Contiguous storage, array decay, multi-dimensional arrays, and the C string convention.

lessons.title: Arrays: a block of memory with a name
lessons.summary: Declaration, indexing, why C has no bounds checking, and the one thing that surprises everyone.

payload.text:
## Declaring an array

```c
int numbers[5];                 /* 5 ints, uninitialised */
int values[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
int partial[5] = {1, 2};         /* -> {1, 2, 0, 0, 0} */
char name[6] = "Hello";          /* -> 5 chars + a terminator */
```

Elements are numbered from 0. An array of 5 has valid indices `0` through `4`. `numbers[5]` is one past the end, and using it is undefined behaviour.

## The layout in memory

An array's elements sit next to each other, in order, with no gaps. That contiguity is the whole point: the CPU can compute any address with one multiply and one add.

```c
int values[4] = {10, 20, 30, 40};
```

| Index | Value | Address |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 10 | base + 0 |
| 1 | 20 | base + 4 |
| 2 | 30 | base + 8 |
| 3 | 40 | base + 12 |

On a system where `int` is 4 bytes. `sizeof values` is 16, and the address of `values[i]` is `&values[0] + i`. This is why arrays are cache-friendly and why the stride is always the element size.

## C does not check your index

This is the single most important thing to internalise.

```c
int values[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
printf("%d\n", values[10]);   /* compiles cleanly. Reads whatever is there. */
```

No warning, no error, no exception. `values[10]` computes `base + 40`, which is 30 bytes past the end of a 20-byte array. If that address is mapped memory, you get garbage. If it is not, the process dies with a segmentation fault. If the array is a local, you have probably just corrupted your own stack frame Ã¢â‚¬â€ the return address, a saved pointer, another local.

The reason is design. Bounds checking in C would cost performance and would not actually help much, because the language cannot know the length of an array passed to a function (see the decay rules below). C made a deliberate trade: the programmer is responsible.

Practical consequences:

- **Initialise your arrays.** `int values[5];` holds indeterminate bytes. Not zeros Ã¢â‚¬â€ indeterminate. Reading them is undefined behaviour, and with optimisations on, the compiler may delete the read entirely.
- **Zero-initialise by default.** `int values[5] = {0};` or `= {}` (C23). This is the single safest habit in C.
- **Use `-Wall` and ASan.** `gcc -fsanitize=address` catches out-of-bounds at the point it happens, with a stack trace.
- **Prefer `static` for large constant tables.**

## sizeof gives you the whole array, in one place

```c
int values[5];
printf("%zu\n", sizeof values);        /* 20 Ã¢â‚¬â€ the whole array */
printf("%zu\n", sizeof values / sizeof values[0]);   /* 5 Ã¢â‚¬â€ the element count */
```

The second line is the standard idiom for "how many elements are in this array", and it works because `sizeof values` is the total bytes and `sizeof values[0]` is the size of one element. The division is integer arithmetic and it is exact.

Note the fragility: this only works where `values` is a genuine array, in a scope where its size is known. As soon as it is passed to a function it becomes a pointer and `sizeof` gives you 8.

## Initialising only part of an array

```c
int zeroes[100] = {0};        /* all 100 elements become 0 */
int sparse[5] = {[2] = 7, [4] = 9};   /* {0, 0, 7, 0, 9} (C99 designated initialisers) */
```

Designated initialisers let you skip the tedious middle. They also work on structs, which is why they are the idiomatic way to set a few fields of a configuration.

## Arrays cannot be assigned

```c
int a[3] = {1, 2, 3};
int b[3] = {4, 5, 6};

a = b;          /* ERROR: invalid operands to binary = */
```

An array is not an assignable value. You cannot copy one array into another with `=`. The two workarounds:

```c
/* 1. copy element by element */
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) a[i] = b[i];

/* 2. use memcpy, which is faster and clearer for bulk copies */
#include <string.h>
memcpy(a, b, sizeof a);
```

The reason is that `a` in almost every context is not really an array Ã¢â‚¬â€ see below. Arrays are not first-class values in C; they are a syntax for a pointer plus a size that the compiler uses at the declaration.

## The array/pointer decay rules

This is the concept that unlocks Module 9, so it is worth getting exactly right.

**Rule 1: in most expressions, an array converts to a pointer to its first element.**

```c
int values[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
int *p = values;      /* fine: p points at values[0] */
printf("%d\n", *values);   /* 1 Ã¢â‚¬â€ values[0], same as *(values + 0) */
```

The conversion happens silently. The array name in an expression is evaluated as `&values[0]`. This is why `values` and `&values[0]` are interchangeable nearly everywhere.

**Rule 2: the exceptions.** The conversion does not happen in:

1. `sizeof values` Ã¢â‚¬â€ the array, not a pointer, so you get the total size.
2. `&values` Ã¢â‚¬â€ gives you a pointer to the *whole array*, of type `int (*)[5]`.
3. A string literal initialising a `char` array Ã¢â‚¬â€ `char s[] = "hi"` is allowed.
4. The operand of the `&` address-of operator, for the same reason as (1).

Everything else Ã¢â‚¬â€ passing to a function, assigning, comparing Ã¢â‚¬â€ sees a pointer.

**Rule 3: a pointer and an array are different types, despite behaving alike.**

```c
int values[5];
int *p = values;         /* OK: array decays to int* */
/* int *q = p;  -- fine, that is a normal pointer copy */
sizeof values            /* 20 */
sizeof p                 /* 8 */
```

The array type `int[5]` carries a size. `int *` does not. That is the only real difference, and it is the reason array parameters need a separate length argument.

## The one-past-the-end pointer

```c
int values[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
int *end = values + 5;    /* legal to FORM */
printf("%d\n", *end);    /* undefined behaviour to DEREFERENCE */
```

Forming a pointer one past the last element is perfectly legal and widely used Ã¢â‚¬â€ half of all pointer arithmetic in real code is `p + 1` until `p == end`. Dereferencing it is not.

This is a natural consequence of the flat address space: `values + 5` is the address right after the array, and there is no runtime check saying that is "outside". The rule exists so that loop comparisons and `end()` iterators in C++ are well-defined.

## Common array mistakes

| Mistake | What happens | Correct |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `int a[5];` then read `a[i]` | Indeterminate garbage, or UB | `int a[5] = {0};` |
| `for (i = 0; i <= 5; i++)` on a 5-element array | Off-by-one on the last iteration | `i < 5` |
| `a = b` | Compile error | `memcpy(a, b, sizeof a)` |
| `int a[n];` then `sizeof a` expecting `n` | Gives the pointer size if `a` was passed to a function | Pass the length |
| Comparing two array names | Compares addresses, never contents | `memcmp`, or loop |
| `int a[5][10];` indexed `a[i][j]` | Correct Ã¢â‚¬â€ row major | Ã¢â‚¬â€ |
| `int a[3] = {1,2,3,4};` | Compile error, too many initialisers | Ã¢â‚¬â€ |

## Passing arrays to functions

Because of decay, the function receives a pointer:

```c
void print_all(const int *values, size_t count)
{
    for (size_t i = 0; i < count; i++) {
        printf("%d ", values[i]);
    }
    putchar('\n');
}

int main(void)
{
    int data[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    print_all(data, 5);          /* length must be passed explicitly */
    return 0;
}
```

Two conventions worth adopting:

1. **Write the parameter as `const int values[]`** (or `const int *values`). It reads as "an array", which is what the caller thinks it is passing, and the `const` documents that you will not modify it.
2. **Always pass the count, as `size_t`.** `int` counts can go negative; `size_t` is unsigned and is the type `sizeof` returns, so no cast is needed at the call site.

payload.title: Five ints in memory

steps.caption: int values[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}; Ã¢â‚¬â€ five ints, declared and initialised.
steps.note: Because the initialiser has exactly five elements, every element is set. Leave one out and the rest become zero.

steps.caption: Each cell is one int, four bytes. On a little-endian machine 10 is stored 0A 00 00 00.
steps.note: The least significant byte is at the lowest address. This is why the bytes of an int are not in the order you read the digits in, and why casting an int* to char* and printing the bytes surprises people.

steps.caption: Indexing is arithmetic. values[3] is computed as base + 3*4 = base + 12.
steps.note: The compiler turns values[i] into *(base + i). This is why indexing an array is exactly as fast as dereferencing a pointer Ã¢â‚¬â€ they are the same operation.

steps.caption: values[5] computes base + 20, which is one past the end of the block.
steps.note: The pointer values + 5 is legal to form and compare. Dereferencing it is undefined behaviour. The C standard promises that one-past-the-end is a valid pointer, not a valid element.

steps.caption: And there is nothing to stop you reading values[99]. No bounds check is generated.
steps.note: This is the deliberate trade in C: no per-access cost, and the programmer owns the invariant. Tools exist to help Ã¢â‚¬â€ compile with -fsanitize=address and the read is caught at the moment it happens.

payload.title: An uninitialised local array holds indeterminate bytes
payload.text: int values[5]; allocates 20 bytes and does not clear them. They contain whatever was on the stack, which is leftover data from previous calls. Reading that is undefined behaviour, and at -O2 the compiler is entitled to assume it does not happen, so it may optimise your check away. Write int values[5] = {0}; Ã¢â‚¬â€ it costs one memset and removes a whole class of bug.

payload.title: Use -Wall and sanitizers while you learn
payload.text: gcc -Wall -Wextra -fsanitize=address,undefined -g program.c. AddressSanitizer catches out-of-bounds reads and writes, use-after-free, and double-free at the moment they occur, and prints a stack trace. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer catches signed overflow, misaligned access, and invalid shifts. They cost runtime, not correctness, and they are the closest thing C has to a borrow checker.

questions.prompt: In C, what does `int values[5];` guarantee about the contents?
options: They are all zero
They are set to the maximum negative value
Nothing Ã¢â‚¬â€ the elements hold indeterminate values
They are set to 1
questions.explanation: Local automatic arrays are uninitialised. Only statics and globals get zero-initialisation. Reading indeterminate values is undefined behaviour.

questions.prompt: Why is `int a[3]; a = a;` a compile error?
options: Because arrays cannot be assigned Ã¢â‚¬â€ the name decays to a pointer, and a pointer is not assignable from a whole array
Because a is const
Because the array is too small
It is legal, and copies element by element
questions.explanation: In an expression, a becomes int*, so a = a assigns a pointer to itself. Copying array contents requires a loop or memcpy.

questions.prompt: What is sizeof p, where `int a[100]; int *p = a;`?
options: 8 on a 64-bit machine (the size of a pointer)
It is undefined
questions.explanation: p is a pointer, so sizeof gives the pointer size. sizeof a gives 400. The difference between the two is exactly the size information that arrays carry and pointers do not.

questions.prompt: Which of these is legal?
options: Dereferencing a pointer to one past the last element
Forming a pointer to one past the last element and comparing it to another pointer in the same array
Reading values[5] on an int values[5]
Assigning one array to another with =
questions.explanation: The standard guarantees one-past-the-end is a valid pointer, so it can be formed, compared and used as an end iterator. Dereferencing it, and indexing the array with the same index, are undefined behaviour.

questions.prompt: What is the standard way to get the element count of `int values[7]` inside the same scope?
options: values.length
sizeof values
sizeof values / sizeof values[0]
It cannot be determined
questions.explanation: The total byte size divided by the size of one element. It works only where the array is a real array Ã¢â‚¬â€ once it decays to a pointer inside a function, it gives 8 / 4 = 2, which is wrong.

lessons.title: Multi-dimensional arrays
lessons.summary: Arrays of arrays, row-major layout, passing them to functions, and the pointer-to-pointer trap.

payload.title: Where a 2D array actually lives

steps.caption: int grid[2][3]; reserves 24 bytes contiguously. There is no runtime object for a 2D array Ã¢â‚¬â€ one flat block that we choose to read in rows.
steps.note: Six cells of 4 bytes each. Every address is on the same ruler: there is no second row of memory below, and no gap between the rows.

steps.caption: grid[0][1] = 2. The compiler computes base + (0*3 + 1)*4 = base + 4.
steps.note: Because the row width 3 is a compile-time constant, this collapses to a single add. That constant is exactly why the second dimension cannot be a function parameter.

steps.caption: grid[1][0] = 4 lands at base + (1*3 + 0)*4 = base + 12 Ã¢â‚¬â€ immediately after grid[0][2].
steps.note: "Row 1" is a way of indexing the block, not a separate object with its own storage. This adjacency is why a flat malloc plus grid[r*cols + c] behaves identically to the 2D syntax.

steps.caption: Because the whole thing is 24 bytes, grid[2][0] is one past the end Ã¢â‚¬â€ formable, not dereferenceable.
steps.note: The flat block gives no second chance. Out-of-range indices land in whatever the next allocation happens to be, which is why -fsanitize=address is worth compiling with while you learn.

payload.title: void f(int grid[]) loses the row width
payload.text: The parameter decays all the way to int *, and the function no longer knows how wide a row is, so it cannot compute the address of grid[1][0]. It is a compile error when you use the two subscripts. Write void f(int grid[][COLS]) Ã¢â‚¬â€ the const version, void f(const int grid[][COLS]), is better still, because it documents that the function does not modify the data.

payload.title: Put array dimensions in constants, not literals
payload.text: enum { ROWS = 8, COLS = 8 }; at the top of the file, then use ROWS and COLS in every declaration, every loop bound, and every function parameter. When a dimension changes, one edit fixes the entire program instead of a hunt through the file for a stray 8.

questions.prompt: Why must the second dimension appear in a 2D array parameter?
options: To allow the compiler to check indices
Because the row width is needed at compile time to compute the address of each row
It is optional, purely for documentation
Because C stores 2D arrays column-major
questions.explanation: The parameter decays to a pointer to a row. The compiler generates *(base + r*width + c), so the width must be a compile-time constant. Omit it and you have a plain int*, which cannot support two subscripts.

questions.prompt: How is grid[1][2] of an `int grid[3][4]` computed?
options: base + (1*2 + 4)*sizeof(int)
base + (1*4 + 2)*sizeof(int)
base + (1 + 2)*sizeof(int)
It requires two pointer dereferences at runtime
questions.explanation: Row major: the row index is multiplied by the full row width, then the column index is added. The compiler flattens the two subscripts into this single expression, so there is one multiply and one add.

questions.prompt: What is `int (*grid)[4];`?
options: An array of 4 pointers to int
A pointer to an array of 4 ints
An array of 4 arrays of int
A 2D array of 4 by 4
questions.explanation: Read right to left from the name: grid is a pointer, to an array, of 4 ints. This is the correct type for a dynamically allocated 2D array with a known column count.

questions.prompt: A VLA is declared as `int data[n];` where n is a runtime value. What is the main practical concern?
options: It does not compile in C89
It is allocated on the stack, so a large n overflows it
It cannot be initialised
It is always slower than malloc
questions.explanation: VLAs are automatic storage duration, so they consume stack. They are ideal for small bounded scratch space and wrong for anything driven by large or untrusted input Ã¢â‚¬â€ use malloc for that.

questions.prompt: Why is `int **grid` with one malloc per row usually worse than one flat malloc?
options: It does not compile in strict C
Rows are separate allocations, so every access is a double dereference, the cache cannot stream across rows, and there are N allocations to free
int ** cannot represent a row
It uses less memory
questions.explanation: A single flat block keeps the rows contiguous, so it is faster and needs one free. The cost is manual index arithmetic, grid[r * cols + c], which the compiler generates anyway for a real 2D array.

lessons.title: C strings: an array of char with a terminator
lessons.summary: The null terminator, why sizeof and strlen differ, safe string functions, and the overflow that started it all.

payload.title: Why sizeof and strlen disagree

steps.caption: char greeting[] = "Hello"; Ã¢â‚¬â€ the compiler sizes the array to fit the literal plus its terminator.
steps.note: Six cells, not five. The array size is known at compile time, so sizeof never reads memory: it is a property of the declaration, not of the contents.

steps.caption: sizeof greeting is 6. strlen(greeting) is 5, because strlen stops at the terminator and does not count it.
steps.note: Two different questions. sizeof asks how much storage the object occupies; strlen asks how many characters precede the first zero byte. They differ by exactly one for any well-formed string.

steps.caption: strlen is that simple: walk from the first byte, counting, until \0.
steps.note: A runtime loop, which is why it costs time proportional to the length Ã¢â‚¬â€ and why it is undefined behaviour if no terminator exists before the end of the object.

steps.caption: Now the same text as a pointer: const char *b = "Hello";
steps.note: The array has already decayed, so there is no array object left for sizeof to measure and it reports the size of the pointer. The string is still 5 characters Ã¢â‚¬â€ only sizeof is now answering a different question.

steps.caption: A buffer needs one byte more than the string length, because the terminator occupies real memory.
steps.note: char buf[6] holds "Hello" exactly. strcpy(buf, "Hello") writes 6 bytes including the terminator. This "+1" is the single most common off-by-one in C, and the reason a 5-character field read with %5s needs 6 bytes.

payload.title: String functions, and what each one gets wrong
rows: Reads past the end if there is no \0
No limit. Overflows if s >= d
Does NOT terminate if s is >= n long
No limit. Overflows if the result exceeds d
Returns a pointer into s, or NULL
Returns the needed length, so you can detect truncation
REMOVED in C11. A guaranteed buffer overflow
Keeps the \n. Returns NULL on error or EOF

payload.title: strncpy does not null-terminate
payload.text: If the source string is at least as long as n, strncpy writes exactly n bytes of source and adds no terminator. The result is a buffer that is not a valid C string, and every function you later call on it will read past the end. Either write dst[n-1] = 0 after the call, or use snprintf, which does both and tells you whether it truncated.

payload.title: Never compare strings with ==
payload.text: == on two char* compares addresses, not contents. Two separately-built strings with identical contents are at different addresses, so the comparison is false. Use strcmp(a, b) == 0. The mirror-image bug is using strcmp(a, b) == 1, which happens to be true on some platforms and false on others Ã¢â‚¬â€ the standard only guarantees the sign.

payload.title: Wrap the dangerous functions once
payload.text: Write str_copy, str_append and str_join helpers with explicit capacity arguments, use them everywhere, and make the unsafe ones static in one file so nobody can reach for them directly. This is what the "safe string" libraries in other languages are really doing Ã¢â‚¬â€ and in C you can write twenty lines and have them for the whole project.

questions.prompt: Why is `sizeof "Hello"` equal to 6?
options: Because the compiler adds a byte for alignment
Because a string literal includes the terminating \0, and sizeof counts every byte of the array
Because sizeof always rounds up to a power of two
It is 5
questions.explanation: The literal is a char[6] Ã¢â‚¬â€ five characters plus the terminator. sizeof counts all six. strlen returns 5 because it stops at the terminator.

questions.prompt: What is `sizeof` of `const char *s = "Hello";`?
options: The size of a pointer, typically 8 on 64-bit
It is undefined
questions.explanation: The array decayed to a pointer when it was assigned, so there is no array to measure. This is the reason sizeof is only meaningful on a genuine array in the same scope.

questions.prompt: You call strncpy(dst, src, sizeof dst) and src is longer than dst. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, it copies sizeof dst bytes safely
dst is not null-terminated, so it is not a valid C string
strncpy always returns NULL
It is a compile error
questions.explanation: strncpy fills the buffer with source bytes and adds no terminator when the source does not fit. Every subsequent string function on dst will read out of bounds.

questions.prompt: Why is `if (a == b)` the wrong way to test whether two char* are equal?
options: It is a compile error
It compares addresses, not the characters they point at
It compares only the first character
It compares lengths
questions.explanation: The pointers were each produced by a separate literal or array, so they have different addresses even when the contents match. Use strcmp(a, b) == 0.

questions.prompt: Why was gets removed from the C standard?
options: It was replaced by a faster function
It reads an unbounded line into a fixed buffer, so it cannot be used without risking overflow
It did not return int
It was buggy on Windows only
questions.explanation: It is impossible to use safely, which is why C11 removed it outright rather than fixing it. Use fgets(buf, sizeof buf, stdin).

modules.title: Module 9 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Pointers
modules.summary: Addresses, dereferencing, the pointer/parameter pass-by-reference idiom, and pointer arithmetic.

lessons.title: What a pointer really is
lessons.summary: An address in a variable. Nothing more mystical than that, and nothing less powerful.

payload.text:
## A pointer is just a number

C has no memory model in a language sense. A pointer is a value that holds an address. That is the entire definition.

```c
int value = 42;
int *p = &value;     /* p holds the address of value */
```

Two operations, and you can do these to any pointer:

```c
&value     /* address-of: where value lives  -> gives int* */
*p         /* dereference: read the value at p -> gives int  */
```

Everything in this module is those two ideas plus arithmetic. When people describe pointers as "dangerous", they usually mean that C will not stop you applying `p + 1` to a pointer that points at nothing.

## Declaring a pointer

```c
int    *p1;      /* pointer to int          */
double *p2;      /* pointer to double       */
char   *p3;      /* pointer to char         */
int   **pp;      /* pointer to pointer      */

int  *arr[5];    /* ARRAY of 5 int pointers      */
int (*arr2)[5];  /* POINTER to an array of 5 ints */
```

The last two lines are the classic trap. **Declarations read right to left, from the name outwards.** `int *arr[5]`: start at `arr`, go right Ã¢â‚¬â€ `[5]` means array; then go left Ã¢â‚¬â€ `int *` means of pointers. So array of pointers. `int (*arr2)[5]`: the parentheses stop the rightward scan, so `arr2` is a pointer, and `(*arr2)` is to an array of 5 ints.

This is why the extra parens are not decoration, and why you should write one or the other with a comment the first time.

## The declaration/init pitfall

```c
int *p = &value;      /* p is the pointer. Correct. */

int *p, q = 5;        /* q is an int, NOT a pointer. Only p is a pointer. */
```

The `*` binds to the declarator, not to the type. It is an easy source of a warning and an easy source of a real bug. The habit that removes it: declare the type, not the pointer, in headers and shared APIs, and keep the `*` attached to the name.

## NULL is not zero, but close

```c
int *p = NULL;        /* the correct way to say "points nowhere" */
if (p == NULL) { ... }

int *q = 0;           /* legal: a null pointer constant. */
```

`NULL` is a macro, usually expanding to `((void*)0)`. Testing against `NULL` rather than `0` is a style preference, not a correctness one Ã¢â‚¬â€ but it documents intent, and it is what every codebase does.

Crucially, the important check is not `p == 0` but whether the pointer is valid at all. See "three pointer flavours" below.

## Why pointers exist

They are not for "saving memory". A pointer is 8 bytes and a struct might be 200. The reasons are:

1. **Pass-by-reference.** C passes every argument by value. To let a function modify the caller's variable, you pass its address. This is the single most common use.
2. **Dynamic memory.** `malloc` hands back an address because it hands back memory whose size is not known at compile time.
3. **Arrays are pointers in disguise.** As Module 8 showed, an array name in an expression *is* a pointer. A working array section requires the pointer concept.
4. **Structures and data structures.** Linked lists, trees, and graphs are built from "this points at the next node", and a pointer is the only way to express that.
5. **Avoiding a copy.** Passing a large struct by value copies it. Passing a pointer to it copies 8 bytes.

## The pass-by-value trap

This is the thing to internalise before anything else. C has exactly one calling convention: everything is copied.

```c
void try_to_change(int x)
{
    x = 999;      /* changes the copy. The caller's x is untouched. */
}

void actually_change(int *x)
{
    *x = 999;     /* writes through the address. The caller's x changes. */
}

int main(void)
{
    int a = 1;
    try_to_change(a);       /* a is still 1 */
    actually_change(&a);    /* a is now 999 */

    int b = 5;
    int *p = &b;
    try_to_change(p);       /* STILL 5. We passed a copy of the pointer. */
    printf("%d\n", b);
}
```

The second result surprises nearly everyone. `try_to_change(p)` copies the *address*, so inside the function `x` is a different pointer variable holding the same value. `x = 999` changes that local pointer to point elsewhere; `b` is untouched. To modify `b` through a pointer parameter you need a pointer to a pointer, or the pattern below.

## Idiomatic pass-by-reference: a return status

Returning "was this successful" as the function's return value, and doing the modification through a pointer parameter, is the C convention:

```c
int set_value(int *out, int new_value)
{
    if (out == NULL) {
        return -1;          /* tell the caller it failed */
    }
    *out = new_value;       /* do the work */
    return 0;
}

int main(void)
{
    int x = 0;

    if (set_value(&x, 42) != 0) {
        fprintf(stderr, "could not set value\n");
    }
    /* x == 42 */
}
```

This gives the caller both an error signal and a written result, with no output parameters chained through the return value. You will see this exact shape in every serious C library.

Note the defensive `NULL` check. A `NULL` pointer that gets written through is a segfault with no diagnostic. The check costs one comparison.

## const on pointers, and the three levels

The direction of `const` matters, and mixing it up is a classic bug:

```c
int value = 10;

int       *p1 = &value;   /* pointer to mutable int             */
const int *p2 = &value;   /* pointer to const int: read only    */
int *const p3 = &value;   /* const pointer: cannot be reseated  */
const int *const p4 = &value;  /* both                          */
```

Reading `int *const p` as a sentence: "p is a const pointer to a mutable int" Ã¢â‚¬â€ you can point p anywhere, but you cannot change what it points at. `p = &other;` fails to compile; `*p = 5;` works.

`const` on a pointer parameter is how you document "this function will not modify your data":

```c
void print_all(const int *values, size_t count);
```

Callers with an `int *` can still pass a pointer-to-const, so the rule is to use `const` in the declaration and it costs the caller nothing.

## Three pointer flavours

Not all pointers are interchangeable, and knowing which you have prevents a whole category of bug:

1. **Null** Ã¢â‚¬â€ `NULL`. Points nowhere. Dereferencing crashes.
2. **Uninitialised** Ã¢â‚¬â€ `int *p;`. Contains whatever was in that stack slot, so it points somewhere random. Testing `if (p == NULL)` on it is meaningless. **Always initialise to `NULL`, always.**
3. **Dangling** Ã¢â‚¬â€ pointed to memory that has been freed or gone out of scope. Dereferencing is undefined behaviour, and this is the most dangerous of the three because the value still looks like a valid address.
4. **Valid** Ã¢â‚¬â€ points into a live object. Fine to dereference, within bounds.

## Dereferencing a NULL crashes, and that is by design

```c
int *p = NULL;
printf("%d\n", *p);      /* segmentation fault */
```

There is no exception, no error code, no message. The program dies. This is a deliberate design point of C: `NULL` dereference is a *bug in your program*, not a runtime condition to be handled, so the language lets it fail immediately and loudly. If it were allowed to continue, the bug would spread.

This is why the `if (out == NULL)` check in every library function is not busywork.

## Pointer arithmetic

C lets you add and subtract integers from pointers. The unit is elements, not bytes.

```c
int values[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};
int *p = values;      /* p -> values[0] */

p + 1                  /* -> values[1], i.e. 4 bytes further on */
p + 2                  /* -> values[2]  */
p - 1                  /* -> one before values[0]: legal to form, illegal to use */
p + 5                  /* one-past-the-end: legal to form, illegal to deref */
```

The compiler scales it for you, using `sizeof *p`. `p + 1` is `(char*)p + 4` on a 4-byte-int machine. You never do that arithmetic by hand.

What is *not* legal is mixing the two: `p + 1.5` is a compile error, and adding a byte offset requires a cast to `char *`:

```c
char *bytes = (char *)p;    /* correct: 1 byte per step */
bytes + 1;                   /* the second byte of the int */
```

## Pointer difference

```c
int *a = values;
int *b = values + 3;
printf("%td\n", b - a);    /* 3 Ã¢â‚¬â€ an element count, not a byte count */
```

The result type is `ptrdiff_t`, and it is the number of elements. `%td` is the correct `printf` specifier for it, or cast to `long` and use `%ld`.

## Assigning to a pointer does not copy the data

```c
int a = 1, b = 2;
int *p = &a;

*p = 100;      /* a becomes 100 */
p = &b;        /* p now points at b. a is still 100. */
```

Two distinct operations that look similar in the source:
- `*p = 100` Ã¢â‚¬â€ write *through* the pointer.
- `p = &b` Ã¢â‚¬â€ move the pointer itself.

`p++` moves the pointer. `(*p)++` increments the pointed-to value. The parentheses matter. This distinction explains most pointer bugs in real code.

## `const` and string literals in one place

```c
const char *version = "1.0";   /* may read, must not write */
char *bad = "1.0";             /* compiles, then crashes on write */
```

A string literal has static storage duration and is usually in read-only memory. The `const` is not optional politeness Ã¢â‚¬â€ it is the only thing that makes the write a compile error instead of a segfault.

## Common pointer mistakes

| Code | Problem |
| --- | --- |
| `int *p;` then `*p = 5;` | `p` is uninitialised; writes to a random address |
| `int *p = NULL; *p = 5;` | Segfault |
| `p = q;` thinking it copies | Copies the address, not the data |
| `a[i] = a[j]` on pointers | Assigns the pointer, not the value |
| `free(p); p = NULL;` omitted | Second use is a dangling pointer |
| `p + 1` on a non-array | Arithmetic is only defined within one array object |
| `strcpy(p, "longer string")` | Overflow; no length known |
| returning `&local;` | The frame is gone; the pointer dangles immediately |

## A practical checklist

- Initialise every pointer to `NULL` at declaration. No exceptions.
- Check every pointer that crosses a function boundary before dereferencing it.
- Prefer `const` in parameters you only read.
- One `free` per `malloc`, and set the pointer to `NULL` immediately after.
- When a pointer points into an array, also keep the end, or the count.
- Compile with `-Wall -Wextra -fsanitize=address` while developing.

payload.title: An uninitialised pointer is not the same as NULL
payload.text: int *p; leaves p holding whatever bytes were at that stack location Ã¢â‚¬â€ typically a return address or a pointer from a previous call. Testing p == NULL on it is meaningless and will usually be false, so the code proceeds and writes to a random address. Declare every pointer as int *p = NULL;. The compiler can then help: it will warn when you dereference a variable that is provably still NULL.

payload.title: Dangling pointers are the hardest bug to find
payload.text: free(p) ends the life of the memory but leaves p holding its old address, and p == NULL is now false. Any later use is undefined behaviour that may not crash for hours. The fix is one line, and it is not optional: free(p); p = NULL;

payload.title: Use a pointer parameter to modify, a pointer-to-const to read
payload.text: void print(const char *s) promises the caller their data is untouched, and any pointer to char converts to it for free. It also stops you from accidentally writing. A const parameter is documentation the compiler enforces Ã¢â‚¬â€ far better than a comment.

questions.prompt: What does `&value` produce?
options: The value stored in `value`
The address of `value`
A copy of `value`
A pointer to a pointer
questions.explanation: The address-of operator gives the address of an object. The dereference operator * is what turns that address back into a value.

questions.prompt: You call `try_to_change(p)` where p points at int b. Inside, the parameter is set to 999. What is b afterwards?
options: 999 Ã¢â‚¬â€ C passes pointers by reference
Unchanged Ã¢â‚¬â€ C passed a copy of the pointer, so only the local copy was modified
Undefined behaviour
0, because the local copy went out of scope
questions.explanation: Everything in C is passed by value, including pointers. The function received its own pointer variable. To change b you need *x = 999, or a pointer-to-pointer if you want the function to reseat the caller pointer.

questions.prompt: How is `p + 1` interpreted when p is an `int *`?
options: As the next byte, so p + 1 points one byte past p
As the next int, i.e. 4 bytes further on a machine with 4-byte ints
As the next pointer, 8 bytes on
It is a compile error
questions.explanation: Pointer arithmetic is in units of the pointed-to type. The compiler scales it by sizeof *p. To step in bytes you cast to char * first.

questions.prompt: What is `int *arr[5];`?
options: An array of 5 pointers to int
A pointer to an array of 5 ints
A 5-element int array
It is a syntax error
questions.explanation: Reading right to left from the name: [5] makes it an array, then int * makes the elements pointers. If you wanted a pointer to an array you would write int (*arr)[5] Ã¢â‚¬â€ the parentheses are what change the meaning.

questions.prompt: Why is `const int *p` different from `int *const p`?
options: They are identical
The first lets you read through p but not write; the second lets you write through p but not reseat p
The first is faster
The second does not compile
questions.explanation: const qualifies whatever it directly precedes. In const int *p the const applies to the int, so p can point anywhere but the data is read-only. In int *const p the const applies to p, so p is locked to one address but that data is writable.

payload.title: Passing an array, and what the callee receives

steps.caption: int data[] = {4, 8, 15, 16, 23, 42}; sits contiguously in memory.
steps.note: Six ints, 24 bytes, no gaps. The compiler knows the length only here, where the array is a real array in a real scope.

steps.caption: reverse(data, n) Ã¢â‚¬â€ inside the function, values is a pointer to data[0]. The array decayed.
steps.note: values[0] still works, because indexing a pointer is the same as *(values + 0). But sizeof values is now 8, not 24. The size is gone unless it is passed separately as count.

steps.caption: The loop swaps values[i] and values[j], with i starting at 0 and j at 5.
steps.note: Two indices walking towards each other, meeting in the middle. This is the standard in-place reversal Ã¢â‚¬â€ it needs no second array and no allocation.

steps.caption: Because the pointer aliases the caller array, every write here is visible to the caller.
steps.note: The function did not get a copy of the data; it got the address of it. That is the entire point of passing a pointer instead of an array.

steps.caption: Done: the caller array is reversed. No return value needed.
steps.note: The effect is visible outside because the function modified the memory through the pointer. A plain array parameter holding a copy would have left the caller unchanged.

payload.title: Do not return the address of a local variable
payload.text: int *bad(void) { int x = 5; return &x; } returns a pointer to a stack frame that no longer exists the instant the function returns. The compiler may well print 5, and then print 5 again, and then print 0. C11 made this official: returning the address of an object with automatic storage duration is undefined behaviour, and many optimisers exploit it. Return a value, or a pointer to something with static or allocated storage.

payload.title: Incrementing a pointer inside a function does not move the callerÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s
payload.text: void advance(int *p) { p++; } changes only the local copy. The caller still holds the original address. If you need to advance the caller pointer, take int **. This is the same pass-by-value rule as before, and it catches everyone once.

payload.title: The parameter trio: pointer, count, and a name for the unit
payload.text: void f(int *values, size_t count) is the shape. Prefer the singular form for pointers and the plural for arrays, and it reads as English. The word you choose for count (n, len, size, capacity) tells the reader whether it is a current length or a maximum, which is not always the same thing.

questions.prompt: What is the standard way for a function to return two int results?
options: Return a struct containing both
Return one and take a pointer parameter for the other, with the function return value used as a status code
Use a global variable
It cannot be done in C
questions.explanation: A status return plus NULL-checked out-parameters is the dominant C convention Ã¢â‚¬â€ it is what div() does. Returning a struct is also valid and sometimes cleaner. A global is never acceptable: it is not reentrant and not thread-safe.

questions.prompt: Why does `void swap_ptrs(int **a, int **b)` need two levels of indirection when `void swap(int *a, int *b)` does not?
options: It does not Ã¢â‚¬â€ both are equally correct
Because swapping pointer values requires writing to the callerÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s pointer variable itself, not to what it points at
Because **a is faster
Because the second form is deprecated

questions.prompt: `const int *p` vs `int *const p`. Which one prevents `p = &other;`?
options: const int *p
int *const p
Neither
Both
questions.explanation: int *const p Ã¢â‚¬â€ the const applies to p, so p is locked to one address. const int *p has a const int, so *p cannot be written, but p can be reseated freely.

questions.prompt: Why does a function parameter declared `int values[]` need a separate count?
options: Because C arrays cannot be passed at all
Because the parameter decays to a pointer and the array size is lost at the call boundary
Because size_t is faster than int
Because the count is needed for bounds checking
questions.explanation: The decay happens at the call, so the callee receives an int* with no size. That is the fundamental limitation of C arrays and the reason every string and buffer function takes a capacity argument.

questions.prompt: What is the danger of `const char *v = "1.0"; v[0] = '2';`?
options: Nothing, the pointer is const
A string literal has static storage duration and is usually read-only, so writing to it is undefined behaviour and typically segfaults
It changes the literal for everyone
The compiler silently fixes it
questions.explanation: The const on the pointer only protects the pointer variable from being reseated. To make the write a compile error you need const char *v Ã¢â‚¬â€ the const must qualify the char, not the pointer.

payload.title: A linked list, built node by node

steps.caption: Queue starts empty: head and tail both NULL, length 0.
steps.note: The struct itself lives on the stack; the nodes live on the heap. The empty state is head == tail == NULL, and that single test answers "is it empty?" everywhere.

steps.caption: queue_push(10): the first node becomes both head and tail.
steps.note: When the list is empty, one node has to be both ends. Miss this and you get a queue where every pop crashes on the second element.

steps.caption: queue_push(20): a new node is appended, and tail is advanced.
steps.note: tail->next = n links the old tail to the new node, then tail = n moves the tail. head stays put, because a queue is FIFO Ã¢â‚¬â€ the front must not move.

steps.caption: queue_push(30): head Ã¢â€ â€™ 10 Ã¢â€ â€™ 20 Ã¢â€ â€™ 30, tail at 30.
steps.note: Three pushes, three nodes, and both ends updated in constant time. The nodes are scattered across the heap, not contiguous Ã¢â‚¬â€ that is the cost of a linked structure, paid back with O(1) insertion.

steps.caption: queue_pop(&out): read the head, unlink it, free it, advance head.
steps.note: Three operations, all O(1). The critical line is reading head->next into a local BEFORE calling free Ã¢â‚¬â€ after the free, that memory is gone, and reading it is a use-after-free.

steps.caption: Pop twice more and the queue is empty: head and tail are NULL again.
steps.note: When head becomes NULL, tail must be set to NULL too. Forgetting that leaves tail pointing at freed memory, and the next push writes through a dangling pointer Ã¢â‚¬â€ a bug that surfaces far from its cause.

payload.text: typedef struct Node { int v; Node *next; } Node; does not compile Ã¢â‚¬â€ "Node" is still being defined, so it is not a complete type and has no known size. Write struct Node *next. The typedef alias is not available until the closing brace, which is exactly why the error is confusing the first time. A forward declaration (struct Node;) elsewhere in the file, or a separate struct for the link, avoids the confusion entirely.

payload.title: Freeing a list while walking it
payload.text: while (head != NULL) { free(head); head = head->next; } is a use-after-free: the statement on the right reads memory that free just returned to the allocator. The fix is to save next first. If the allocator reuses that memory immediately Ã¢â‚¬â€ which many do Ã¢â‚¬â€ the loop can walk into a cycle and run forever instead of crashing, which is far harder to debug.

payload.title: A queue that keeps both head and tail is a real design decision
payload.text: With only a head, every dequeue is O(n): you must walk to find the last node to relink it. Storing the tail makes push and pop both O(1) at the cost of one more invariant to maintain Ã¢â‚¬â€ the tail must be cleared when the queue empties. When you add a fast path, you also add a state you must keep consistent. Write the invariant in a comment.

questions.prompt: Why must a self-referential struct use `struct Node *next;` and not `Node *next;`?
options: To keep the struct small
Because inside its own definition the tag is not yet a complete type, so its size is unknown
Because the typedef is a different type

Because after free, head->next is a use-after-free read

questions.prompt: What does `malloc(sizeof *n)` do when n is a `Node *`, and why is that form preferred?
