questions.prompt: A singly linked list supports which operation in constant time without a tail pointer?
options: Finding the last node
Prepending a new node at the head
Appending at the tail
Removing a node in the middle
questions.explanation: Prepending needs to touch only the new node and the head pointer. Appending needs the last node, which requires a walk; removing from the middle needs the previous node, which also requires a walk. Both become O(1) if you keep tail, or a doubly-linked list with a prev link.

questions.prompt: What tool reports the exact source line of a use-after-free, with a stack trace?

lessons.title: The heap, and why it exists
lessons.summary: Automatic versus dynamic storage, and the one question that decides which you need.

payload.title: Stack and heap are different regions

steps.caption: Automatic variables live on the stack. When a function returns, its whole frame is popped and that memory is reused.
steps.note: The stack is fast because allocation is just moving a pointer. Its limit is that a frame cannot outlive its function Ã¢â‚¬â€ which is exactly why a pointer to a local is a dangling pointer the moment the function returns.

steps.caption: malloc carves a block out of the heap. The block has no scope Ã¢â‚¬â€ it lives until free is called.
steps.note: That is the entire point of the heap: the lifetime is decided by you, not by the shape of the call graph.

steps.caption: f() returns. Its stack frame is gone Ã¢â‚¬â€ but the heap block is untouched, because free has not been called.
steps.note: A pointer returned from f remains valid. This is how functions return dynamically sized data: the data does not live in the frame.

steps.caption: free releases the block. The heap slot is now available to the next malloc.
steps.note: The pointer variable still holds the old address Ã¢â‚¬â€ it is now dangling. Setting it to NULL immediately is what keeps a later accidental use from reading reused memory.

steps.caption: Forget the free and the block is leaked: unreachable but still reserved, for the life of the process.
steps.note: A leak is not a crash, which is why it survives review. In a web server handling requests, a leak of a few kilobytes per request becomes gigabytes per day.

payload.title: The four dynamic-memory bugs

payload.title: Never cast the result of malloc
payload.text: int *p = (int *)malloc(n); compiles in C, and in C it is worse than pointless: the cast hides the missing declaration of malloc, so if you forget #include <stdlib.h> the compiler assumes malloc returns int, and on a 64-bit machine that truncates the pointer. Without the cast, the same mistake is a warning or an error. In C++, the cast is required Ã¢â‚¬â€ which is one of the clearest signs the two languages are not the same.

payload.title: One allocation, one free Ã¢â‚¬â€ write the owner in a comment
payload.text: A comment on the function declaration such as "Returns a mallocÃ¢â‚¬â„¢d buffer; caller frees" or "Takes ownership of p" is the cheapest memory-safety documentation there is. The rule of thumb: whoever mallocs frees, or the name says otherwise.

questions.prompt: What is the essential difference between automatic and allocated storage?
options: Allocated storage is faster
Automatic storage is freed when the block ends; allocated storage lives until free is called and its size can be chosen at runtime
Automatic storage is heap memory
Allocated storage cannot be passed to functions
questions.explanation: The two defining properties of the heap are runtime size and lifetime that spans function calls. If you do not need either, a local is simpler and cannot leak.

questions.prompt: Why does `calloc(n, size)` avoid a class of overflow bug that `malloc(n * size)` does not?
options: It is faster
It checks whether n*size overflows and returns NULL instead of allocating a too-small block
It zeroes the memory
It does not Ã¢â‚¬â€ they are identical
questions.explanation: malloc(n*size) computes the product in size_t and can wrap, allocating a tiny block that your code then overflows. calloc performs the multiplication internally with an overflow check, which is a real security advantage. It also zeroes, which is a separate benefit.

questions.prompt: What is a dangling pointer?
options: A pointer that has been assigned NULL
A pointer that still holds the address of memory that has been freed or gone out of scope
A pointer with a syntax error
A pointer to static storage
questions.explanation: The memory is gone but the pointer still names it. Dereferencing is undefined behaviour, and it is the most dangerous pointer state because the value still looks valid.

questions.prompt: What is the immediate consequence of freeing the same pointer twice?
options: Nothing, free is idempotent
The second free is fine and returns an error code
The allocatorÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s bookkeeping is corrupted, producing a crash or exploit later, far from the double free
The C runtime raises an exception
questions.explanation: free is not idempotent. A double free corrupts the allocatorÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s free-list, and the damage surfaces at the next unrelated allocation. Setting the pointer to NULL after freeing turns a double free into a harmless free(NULL).

questions.prompt: A function returns a pointer to one of its local variables. Why is this wrong?
options: It is fine as long as the caller reads it immediately
The local has automatic storage, so it is destroyed when the function returns and the pointer is immediately dangling
Because local variables are const
It wastes stack space
questions.explanation: The frame is popped on return. Returning &local is undefined behaviour even if the value happens to survive, and the compiler is allowed to exploit that. Return a value, a static buffer, or a heap allocation.

lessons.summary: Growing a buffer correctly, handling the classic realloc leak, and building a vector of your own.

payload.title: Growing a vector by doubling

steps.caption: vec_init(&v, 0): no allocation yet. data is NULL, length 0, capacity 0.
steps.note: A vector can start empty and allocate on first push. This avoids a malloc for the common case of an empty container that is never filled.

steps.caption: First push: reserve(1) sees capacity 0, so it allocates 1 element. data is non-NULL.
steps.note: realloc(NULL, n) is guaranteed to behave as malloc(n), so the same growth routine handles both the first allocation and every later one.

steps.caption: Second push: length+1 (2) exceeds capacity (1). Double to 2 and realloc.
steps.note: The data may be copied to a new address. That is why the realloc result must go into a temporary first, and why any other pointer into the old block becomes invalid after growth.

steps.caption: Fifth push: capacity doubles 2 Ã¢â€ â€™ 4 Ã¢â€ â€™ 8. Capacity is always >= length.
steps.note: The gap between length and capacity is wasted space by design: it is the room for the next pushes, and it is what makes the amortised cost O(1) instead of O(n) per element.

steps.caption: vec_free sets data to NULL and both counters to 0. The vector is reusable and cannot be double-freed.
steps.note: Resetting the struct after free is what lets free(NULL) absorb a second vec_free call, and it prevents a stale data pointer from being pushed to later.

payload.title: The realloc leak: never assign straight back to the pointer
payload.text: p = realloc(p, n); if (realloc fails, it returns NULL, p is overwritten with NULL, and the original block is leaked with no way to reach it. Always realloc into a temporary and assign only on success. This exact line appears in production code, and it takes a Valgrind run on the failure path to see it.

payload.title: Grow geometrically, never by one
payload.text: Doubling gives amortised O(1) per push. Growing by one element per push reallocates and copies every time, which is O(n) per push and O(nÃ‚Â²) overall. For ten thousand elements that is the difference between microseconds and a second. Choose 1.5x to 2x and justify it once in a comment.

questions.prompt: What does `realloc` do on failure?
options: Frees the original block and returns NULL
Returns NULL and leaves the original block allocated and untouched
Returns a smaller block
Aborts the program
questions.explanation: It leaves the original alone, which is why assigning the result directly to the only pointer to the block leaks it. Use a temporary and assign only on success.

questions.prompt: Why does the vector grow capacity geometrically rather than by one?
options: To use more memory
Because doubling gives amortised O(1) per push, while growing by one is O(n) per push
Because realloc requires a power of two
It does not matter
questions.explanation: Each element is copied O(1) times on average when capacity doubles: n/2 + n/4 + ... sums to n. Growing by one copies the whole array every push, which is quadratic overall.

questions.prompt: In a vector, what is the difference between length and capacity?
options: They are the same
Length is the number of elements in use; capacity is the number of slots allocated
Capacity is the number of elements in use; length is the allocated size
Length is in bytes
questions.explanation: Elements below length are initialised and valid to read. Slots between length and capacity are allocated but uninitialised, and reading them is a bug.

questions.prompt: What is `realloc(NULL, n)` equivalent to?
options: free(NULL)
malloc(n)
calloc(1, n)
It is undefined behaviour
questions.explanation: The standard guarantees it behaves as malloc. This is what lets a single reserve routine handle both the first allocation and every subsequent growth.

questions.prompt: You have `char **lines` where each lines[i] is a separate mallocÃ¢â‚¬â„¢d string. What is the correct free order?
options: free(lines), then free each lines[i]
free each lines[i], then free(lines)
Only free(lines); the strings are inside it
free(lines, count)
questions.explanation: Free the inner allocations first while you can still reach them, then the array. Freeing the array first loses the string pointers and leaks every string.

lessons.title: Memory bugs, ownership, and the tools that find them
lessons.summary: Use-after-free, double-free, and overflow Ã¢â‚¬â€ reproduced, then caught with ASan and Valgrind.

payload.text:
## What "unsafe" actually means

Every memory bug in C comes from the same root: **a pointer is trusted, and nothing checks that it is still valid.** There is no borrow checker and no garbage collector. The compiler checks types, not lifetimes.

The practical approach is not to be careful (nobody is, reliably). It is to (a) follow a small set of ownership rules and (b) run tools that catch violations the moment they happen.

## Use after free, reproduced

```c
int *p = malloc(sizeof *p);
*p = 42;
free(p);
printf("%d\n", *p);    /* UNDEFINED BEHAVIOUR */
```

This often prints 42. That is the trap: the memory is usually still addressable, and the allocator has not yet reused it. The program looks correct. Then a later allocation reuses the block and the value changes, or the allocator unmaps the page and you get a segfault Ã¢â‚¬â€ in a function with no obvious connection to the original bug.

ASan catches it at the exact read:

```
==12345==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address 0x602000000010
READ of size 4 at 0x602000000010 thread T0
    #0 0x... in main use_after_free.c:7
freed by thread T0 here:
    #0 0x... in free
    #1 0x... in main use_after_free.c:6
```

It prints both where the memory was freed and where it was used. That pair is what makes ASan worth the compile time. No amount of staring at the source gives you the same information.

## Double free, and why the crash is late

```c
int *p = malloc(sizeof *p);
free(p);
free(p);        /* the allocator's free-list is now corrupted */
```

The immediate effect is not the crash. The allocator writes the block into its free list, and on the second free it writes it again Ã¢â‚¬â€ so the free list now has a cycle, or two pointers to the same block. The crash happens on the **next** `malloc`, which walks a corrupt list. That is why double-free bugs are so expensive to locate without a tool. ASan reports the second free immediately.

## The fix that costs one line

```c
free(p);
p = NULL;
free(p);        /* now free(NULL), which is a guaranteed no-op */
```

The standard says `free(NULL)` does nothing. Setting the pointer to `NULL` after freeing makes every later free of the same pointer harmless, and every later dereference a clean crash at the bug site. **Adopt this as a reflex.** It removes double-free and shortens the distance to every use-after-free.

## Heap overflow

```c
char *buf = malloc(10);
strcpy(buf, "this is far too long for ten bytes");   /* overflow */
```

The write runs past the block into the allocator's metadata or the next allocation. Consequences, in increasing severity:

- The adjacent allocation's contents are corrupted (a subtle wrong-answer bug).
- The allocator's metadata is corrupted (a crash on free).
- A crafted overflow overwrites a function pointer or return address (code execution).

This is the mechanism behind a large fraction of real-world exploits. The C string functions that do not take a length are exactly the ones to avoid; the Module 8 rule applies directly here.

## Reading uninitialised memory

```c
int *p = malloc(sizeof *p);
printf("%d\n", *p);     /* uninitialised: UB, and at -O2 the read may vanish */
```

`malloc` does not zero. Valgrind reports "Conditional jump or move depends on uninitialised value(s)" and points at the branch that used it. `calloc` removes the problem for the cost of one memset.

## The ownership model, stated once

Everything above is prevented by one invariant, applied consistently:

> **Every allocated block has exactly one owner. The owner is the code that calls `free`. Ownership can be transferred (returned from a function, stored in a struct), but never duplicated except with an explicit, documented shared-ownership scheme.**

In practice:

- A function that mallocs and returns transfers ownership to the caller Ã¢â‚¬â€ document it.
- A function that receives a pointer for temporary use does not take ownership Ã¢â‚¬â€ do not free it.
- A struct that owns a block frees it in its destroy function.
- Two pointers to one block is fine as long as the `free` happens in one place.

This single rule answers "who frees this?" for every pointer in the program, and "who frees this?" is the question that leaks come from.

## The tools

### AddressSanitizer (ASan)

```
gcc -fsanitize=address -fsanitize=undefined -g -O1 program.c
```

Detects, at the moment of the operation, with a stack trace:

- Heap and stack buffer overflow
- Use after free / return
- Double free and invalid free
- Use of uninitialised memory (with `-fsanitize=memory` in Clang)

Cost is roughly 2x time and memory. Use it in development and CI. There is no reason to ship a C project without an ASan build in the test matrix.

### Valgrind

```
valgrind --leak-check=full --track-origins=yes ./program
```

Slower (10-30x), but it finds things ASan alone does not, in particular **leaks**. It reports each leaked block with the allocation stack trace:

```
definitely lost: 40 bytes in 1 blocks
   at 0x...: malloc
   by 0x...: main (program.c:12)
```

"Definitely lost" is a leak with no remaining pointer; "still reachable" is memory held by a global or static pointer at exit, which is often intentional.

### UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (UBSan)

Included with `-fsanitize=undefined`. Catches signed integer overflow, invalid shifts, misaligned access, null dereference, and more Ã¢â‚¬â€ the class of bug that has no memory symptom at all until the optimiser uses it as an excuse.

### The compiler

```
gcc -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Wconversion -O2
```

Not a substitute for the runtime tools, but free and catches a large fraction of mistakes before they run. Treat warnings as errors in new code.

## A debugging recipe

When memory misbehaves, in order:

1. **Rebuild with `-fsanitize=address,undefined -g -O1`.** Run the same input. In most cases ASan names the line.
2. **Run Valgrind** if ASan is clean but memory grows, or if the report is confusing. `--track-origins=yes` for uninitialised values.
3. **Print the pointers.** `printf("%p\n", (void*)p);` before and after each suspect operation. A pointer that becomes `(nil)` or changes unexpectedly tells you which line is responsible.
4. **GDB watchpoints** for corruption that no sanitizer has pinned down: `watch *(int*)0xADDRESS`, then `continue` until the write that changes it.
5. **Bisect the code.** Comment out half. The bug is in the half that still fails. This is unglamorous and effective.

## Which bugs each tool finds

| Bug | ASan | Valgrind | UBSan | Compiler |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Buffer overflow | yes | yes | no | sometimes |
| Use after free | yes | yes | no | no |
| Double free | yes | yes | no | no |
| Memory leak | yes (LSan) | yes | no | no |
| Uninitialised read | no | yes | no | sometimes |
| Signed overflow | no | no | yes | no |
| Invalid shift | no | no | yes | sometimes |
| Use of a dangling stack pointer | yes | yes | no | sometimes |

Run all four in the development loop. Between them they catch nearly everything.

## Why this module matters more than the syntax

Writing a program that compiles is not the same as writing a correct one. In C specifically, the gap between "it compiled and ran once" and "it is correct" is almost entirely memory behaviour. That is why the tools are not optional extras for this language Ã¢â‚¬â€ they are the discipline.

The three habits, once more:

1. **Initialise** everything Ã¢â‚¬â€ pointers to `NULL`, arrays to `{0}`, mallocs checked.
2. **One owner** per allocation; document ownership on every function that allocates or transfers.
3. **Sanitize** Ã¢â‚¬â€ `-fsanitize=address,undefined` in development and in CI.

payload.title: The four memory bugs, one at a time
payload.code:
int  *p = malloc(sizeof *p);   /* 1: allocate */
*p = 42;                     /* 2: use      */
free(p);                     /* 3: release  */

/* ---- each line below is a bug in a different program ---- */

printf("%d", *p);            /* use after free   */
free(p);                     /* double free      */
char *b = malloc(4);
strcpy(b, "teach");          /* heap overflow    */
printf("%d", *b);            /* uninitialised    */

steps.caption: Allocate: malloc returns a block. p is its only name.
steps.note: The block is uninitialised. At this point the program is correct: it owns 4 usable bytes.

steps.caption: Use: *p = 42 writes within the block. Still correct.
steps.note: The written value lives in the heap block, not in p. p holds the address; the block holds the data.

steps.caption: free(p): the block returns to the allocator. p still holds the address Ã¢â‚¬â€ it is now dangling.
steps.note: The one-line fix is p = NULL; here. Without it, every later use of p is undefined behaviour that may not crash for a long time.

steps.caption: Bug 1 Ã¢â‚¬â€ use after free: *p reads memory that no longer belongs to the program.
steps.note: It may print 42, because the allocator has not reused the block yet. That is not correctness Ã¢â‚¬â€ it is undefined behaviour that happened to work. ASan reports heap-use-after-free with the free site and the read site.

steps.caption: Bug 2 Ã¢â‚¬â€ double free: the block is written to the free list a second time.
steps.note: No crash here. The free list is now corrupt, and the crash arrives at the next malloc, in an unrelated function. This is why double frees are so costly to find by eye.

steps.caption: Bug 3 Ã¢â‚¬â€ heap overflow: strcpy writes 6 bytes into a 4-byte block and corrupts the metadata after it.
steps.note: The overflow lands in the allocatorÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s header or the next allocation. A targeted version overwrites a return address, which is how buffer overflows become exploits.

steps.caption: Bug 4 Ã¢â‚¬â€ uninitialised read: *b prints whatever bytes happened to be there.
steps.note: malloc does not zero. Valgrind reports a read of an uninitialised value and traces it to this line. calloc would have made it zero.

payload.title: free(NULL) is safe; free(garbage) is not
payload.text: The standard guarantees free(NULL) does nothing, which is what makes "pointer = NULL after free" so useful. What is not safe is freeing a pointer that was never returned by malloc, or that has already been freed and not set to NULL, or that points into the middle of a block. All of those are undefined behaviour and all of them corrupt the allocator.

payload.title: Put the sanitizers in CI, not just in habits
payload.text: A -fsanitize=address,undefined build running the test suite catches memory bugs the day they are introduced, not the day they page someone. The same is true of valgrind --leak-check=full on a long-running integration test. Discipline alone does not survive a deadline; a failing build does.

questions.prompt: Why is use-after-free not reliably caught by testing without a tool?
options: It always crashes immediately
The freed memory usually still holds the old value, so the program appears to work until the allocator reuses the block
It is a compile error
The compiler removes the access
questions.explanation: The block is still addressable and usually unreused, so the stale value is read back. The bug becomes visible only under a different allocation pattern or with a sanitizer that marks the memory poisoned.

questions.prompt: What is the correct immediate fix after `free(p)`?
options: Set p = NULL so a later free is a no-op and a later use is a clean crash
Call free again to be sure
Nothing is needed
questions.explanation: free(NULL) is a guaranteed no-op, and a NULL dereference crashes at the bug site. Both properties are what make the one-liner worth doing every time.

questions.prompt: Which tool finds a memory leak AND prints the allocation stack trace?
options: The compiler with -Wall
Valgrind with --leak-check=full
UBSan
A printf after every malloc
questions.explanation: ValgrindÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s leak checker reports each leaked block with the malloc call stack. ASan can also detect leaks (LeakSanitizer) and is faster. UBSan finds arithmetic and alignment undefined behaviour, not leaks.

questions.prompt: A heap buffer overflow can lead to code execution because it can:
options: Slow the program down
Overwrite the allocatorÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s metadata or a return address with attacker-controlled bytes
Change the source code
Free memory automatically
questions.explanation: The written data extends past the intended block into adjacent memory that the allocator or the call stack uses. Carefully chosen bytes can corrupt a pointer or return address, which is the classic exploit primitive.

questions.prompt: What is the single ownership rule that prevents most memory bugs?
options: Always use calloc
Every allocated block has exactly one owner, and the owner frees it
Never use pointers
Free everything at program exit
questions.explanation: One owner means one free, which removes leaks (the owner always frees), double frees (only one site frees), and clarifies the contract for every function that passes a pointer around.

modules.title: Module 11 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Structs, unions, enums, and typedef
modules.summary: Composite types, memory layout and padding, bit-fields, tagged unions, and naming types well.

lessons.title: Structs: grouping related data
lessons.summary: Definition, declaration, initialisation, accessing, and passing by value versus pointer.

payload.title: A struct is just its members, laid out in order

steps.caption: struct Point { int x; int y; double d; }; = {1, 2, 1.0}. Members appear in declaration order.
steps.note: The first member is at the lowest address. This is guaranteed by the standard in the sense that a pointer to the struct, suitably converted, points at the first member.

steps.caption: x and y are two ints, 4 bytes each. No padding needed between them: both are aligned to 4.
steps.note: Each member must start at an address that is a multiple of its alignment. int needs 4-byte alignment, and 0x400104 is a multiple of 4, so y follows x directly.

steps.caption: double needs 8-byte alignment. The next free address, 0x400108, is not a multiple of 8, so 4 bytes of padding are inserted.
steps.note: That padding is not part of any member and holds indeterminate bytes. This is why ordering members from largest alignment to smallest usually reduces sizeof.

steps.caption: d lives at 0x400110, the first 8-aligned address. sizeof(struct Point) is 16, not 14.
steps.note: The struct size is rounded up to its strictest member alignment so that an array of the struct keeps every element aligned. Never assume sizeof equals the sum of the members.

steps.caption: Reorder to { double d; int x; int y; } and the padding moves to the tail, giving the same 16 with no interior hole.
steps.note: Place the widest-aligned members first and the total is often unchanged but the layout is cleaner, and for larger structs the saving is real. This is a compiler-independent win with no change in behaviour.

payload.title: Struct operations and their semantics
rows: Set named members, zero the rest

payload.title: memcmp on structs is not a valid equality test
payload.text: Padding bytes have indeterminate values, so two structs that are logically equal member-by-member can differ in the padding and fail memcmp. Floating-point types can also have multiple bit patterns for the same value (and padding inside them). Compare field by field. This is why C refuses to give you == for structs: the compiler cannot know which bytes are meaningful.

payload.title: Order struct members from largest alignment to smallest
payload.text: Putting doubles and pointers first, then ints, then chars, often removes interior padding at no cost. It is a free optimisation that changes no behaviour and no interface, and on large arrays of structs the memory and bandwidth savings are significant. Check with sizeof before and after.

questions.prompt: `struct Point a = {1, 2};` then `struct Point b = a; b.x = 99;`. What is a.x?
options: 99, because b is a reference to a
1, because struct assignment makes an independent memberwise copy
Undefined
questions.explanation: Struct assignment copies every member. b is a separate object. This is different from array assignment, which does not exist at all.

questions.prompt: Why is `p->x` the same as `(*p).x`?
options: It is a coincidence
Because -> is defined as dereference-then-select; the parentheses are required in the long form because . binds tighter than *
Because p is an array
Because of operator overloading
questions.explanation: The long form needs parentheses: *p.x would be *(p.x). The -> operator exists precisely to avoid writing the parentheses.

questions.prompt: A struct contains an `int x; int y; double d;` in that order. Why might `sizeof` be 16 instead of 14?
options: The compiler adds a sentinel
Padding is inserted so double starts at an 8-byte-aligned address, and the total is rounded to the strictest alignment
sizeof always rounds up to a power of two
The struct stores its own metadata
questions.explanation: 4 bytes of padding between y and d align the double at offset 8. The total 16 is a multiple of 8 so that an array of the struct keeps every element aligned.

questions.prompt: What is the danger of passing a struct that owns a heap pointer by value?
options: It is slower
The copy duplicates the pointer, so two structs own the same block and a double free becomes likely
It does not compile
The pointer is set to NULL in the original
questions.explanation: The copy is shallow: the pointer value is duplicated, not the pointed-to data. Freeing through both structs is a double free, and copying through either aliases the other. Pass by pointer, or implement an explicit deep copy.

questions.prompt: How do you declare a function that returns a pointer to a struct whose definition is hidden from callers?
options: It cannot be done in C
Forward-declare the struct Ã¢â‚¬â€ `struct Database;` Ã¢â‚¬â€ and declare functions taking and returning `struct Database *`
Use void * only
Include the full definition in the header
questions.explanation: An incomplete type is enough to declare pointers to it. The definition stays in the .c file. This is CÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s encapsulation mechanism.

lessons.title: typedef, enums, and unions
lessons.summary: Naming types, named integer constants, and the type that stores one thing at a time.

payload.title: A tagged union: one storage, a tag decides the view

steps.caption: struct Value stores an int64 tag plus a union of long, double, and char*. sizeof is at least 16.
steps.note: The union is 8 bytes (the largest member) and the tag is 4, so the struct is 16 with padding. Storage is reserved for the widest member even when a smaller one is live.

steps.caption: Write v.kind = K_INT and v.u.i = 42. Only the long view is meaningful.
steps.note: The tag says which member is live. Nothing enforces this at the language level; the code must write the tag every time it writes the union, and check it before every read.

steps.caption: Write v.kind = K_REAL and v.u.r = 3.14. The same 8 bytes now hold a double.
steps.note: Writing one member overwrites the bytes of the previous member. The old integer value is gone Ã¢â‚¬â€ a union stores one value, it does not store all of them.

steps.caption: Read u.i now and you get the low 32 bits of the double reinterpreted as an int Ã¢â‚¬â€ a bug, not a feature.
steps.note: This is why the tag is mandatory. Without it, there is no way to know which member is live, and any read of the wrong member is either implementation-defined or undefined behaviour.

steps.caption: Free only the live member. value_free checks kind == K_STR before freeing u.s.
steps.note: Freeing a union member that is not live frees a garbage pointer. The tag-driven destroy is the mirror image of the tag-driven read, and both must be written together.

payload.title: typedef, enum, and union at a glance
rows: No new type, no type safety
The tag is required inside the body
Constants are int; enum Color c = 42 is legal
Pin values that cross a boundary
Only the last-written member is valid
Tag written on set, checked on read

payload.title: Typedef does not create a distinct type
payload.text: typedef int Seconds; and typedef int Metres; are the same type as each other and as int. Your function taking Seconds accepts Metres, and the compiler says nothing. If you need real type safety between two quantities, wrap them in a struct, use an opaque handle, or accept the discipline of the naming convention. C has no strong typedef.

payload.title: Unions are only safe with a tag
payload.text: A bare union has no way to know which member is live. Reading the wrong member reinterprets the same bytes as a different type, which is usually undefined behaviour. Every union that is read at more than the point of assignment should carry a discriminator, and every read should be guarded by it.

payload.title: Use enum for sets of constants, #define for macros only
payload.text: An enum is a real symbol: typed, scoped, and visible in the debugger. A #define is a text substitution with no type and no scope. Reach for enum for constants that belong together, and reserve #define for genuine compile-time macros and include guards.

questions.prompt: What does `typedef struct { int x; } Point;` actually create?
options: A new type distinct from every other
An alias Point for an anonymous struct type
A variable named Point
A macro
questions.explanation: typedef introduces a name for an existing type. It does not create a distinct type, so two typedefs of the same underlying type are interchangeable to the compiler.

questions.prompt: In C, `enum Color c = 42;` Ã¢â‚¬â€ what happens?
options: A compile error
It compiles; an enum variable can hold any int value
c becomes the largest enumerator
Undefined behaviour at runtime
questions.explanation: C enums are integers with named constants and no range enforcement. Use -Wswitch-enum and a default/assert to catch invalid values at the boundaries where they can enter.

questions.prompt: What is the size of `union U { char c; int i; double d; };`?
options: 13, the sum of the members
8, the largest member rounded to the strictest alignment
It is implementation-defined and unpredictable
questions.explanation: All members share the same start, so the union must be big enough for the largest one and aligned to the strictest Ã¢â‚¬â€ here 8 for the double.

questions.prompt: Why is a tagged union safer than a bare union?
options: It uses less memory
The tag records which member is live, so reads can be guarded against the correct type
It allows comparing unions with ==
It prevents all undefined behaviour automatically
questions.explanation: The tag is written when a member is set and checked before any read. This is how C models "one of several types" and it is the pattern behind every dynamic-value representation.

questions.prompt: What is the portable way to reinterpret a float as its 32-bit integer representation?
options: int i = *(int *)&f;
union { float f; int i; } u; u.f = 1.0f; return u.i;
memcpy into an int variable
It cannot be done in C
questions.explanation: memcpy is the sanctioned, strict-aliasing-safe conversion, and compilers optimise it to a register move. Casting a float* to int* and dereferencing violates strict aliasing; reading a different union member is implementation-defined except through char.
