questions.prompt: Inside a function, `print(x)` is on line 2 and `x = 1` is on line 4, and there is a module-level `x = 0`. What happens when the function is called?
options: It prints `0` and then creates a local `x`
It prints `0` and assigns 1 to the module-level `x`
It raises `NameError`, because `x` does not exist in any local scope
It raises `UnboundLocalError` before printing anything
questions.explanation: Python decides a name is local for the entire function the moment an assignment to it appears in the body Ã¢â‚¬â€ not from the line of the assignment onward. So the `x` on line 2 is a local slot that has not been filled, and the read fails before `print` runs. Fix it with `global x` or, far better, by taking `x` as a parameter.

questions.prompt: When Python evaluates `obj.name`, and the class defines `name` as a `property` while the instance dictionary also has a `name` entry, which one is used?
options: The instance dictionary, because instance data is always checked before the class
The property, because data descriptors found on the type take priority over the instance dictionary
Whichever was assigned most recently
The class attribute, and the instance entry is silently ignored
questions.explanation: The full rule is: data descriptors on the type first, then the instance `__dict__`, then non-data descriptors and plain class attributes. Because a `property` is a data descriptor, defining one makes the attribute read-only no matter what is in the instance dictionary Ã¢â‚¬â€ while a plain function attribute loses to the instance dictionary. `__getattribute__` is the hook that implements the whole search.

questions.prompt: What does `nonlocal` let you do that `global` does not?
options: Rebind a name in the nearest enclosing function scope, so an inner function can update an outer functionÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s local without touching the module namespace
Make a name global from inside a class body
Remove the need for `return` in a generator function
Delete a name as well as assign to it
questions.explanation: `global` reaches the module namespace. `nonlocal` reaches the nearest enclosing *function* scope, skipping the current one. It exists for closures and accumulators Ã¢â‚¬â€ `def make_accumulator(): total = 0; def add(n): nonlocal total; total += n; return add` Ã¢â‚¬â€ and reading a name you never assign does not need either declaration.

questions.prompt: What does `gen.send(value)` do, and when is it legal?
options: It raises `value` as an exception inside the generator
It replaces the generator object with a new one
It resumes a suspended generator and makes the `yield` expression that suspended it evaluate to `value`
It returns the generatorÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s `return` value immediately
questions.explanation: The argument of `send` becomes the result of the `yield` expression that the generator is currently sitting on Ã¢â‚¬â€ which is what makes it the basis of coroutines. `send(None)` is exactly `next(gen)`, and calling `send` on a just-started generator raises `TypeError: can't send non-None value to a just-started generator`, because there is no suspended `yield` to deliver it to.

questions.prompt: Which of these builds the whole list immediately, and which defers all work until iteration?
options: `list(f(x) for x in data)` defers; `f(x) for x in data` is eager
`[f(x) for x in data]` is eager; `f(x) for x in data` is lazy
Both are eager, because both fully evaluate `f` before continuing
Both are lazy, because the parentheses are only grouping
questions.explanation: The brackets construct a real `list`, running every element right now. The parentheses construct a generator object that merely holds the loop. Over a large or unbounded source that is the difference between exhausting memory and holding a constant footprint, and `sum(f(x) for x in data)` avoids the intermediate list entirely. If you want eager, use a list comprehension Ã¢â‚¬â€ never `list()` over a generator, which is just a slower comprehension.

questions.prompt: Inside an `except` block, `raise TaskError(msg) from exc` does what?
options: Suppresses `exc` so that only the new error is reported
Retries the `except` block using the new exception type
Converts `exc` into a `TaskError` in place
Raises a new `TaskError` and sets its `__cause__` to `exc`, so the traceback shows both and names the new error as the direct cause
questions.explanation: Even without `from`, Python chains the two exceptions: the new one gets `__context__` pointing at the old one, and the traceback prints "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred". The explicit `from` sets `__cause__` instead and changes the wording to "The above exception was the direct cause". Use it when the new failure is *caused by* the old; leave it implicit when the old is only background context.

questions.prompt: Why does a `with` block call `__exit__` when the body raises?
options: The statement is compiled as `try`/`finally`; `__exit__` receives the exception info, and returning a truthy value from it suppresses the exception
`__exit__` is called before the body runs, so resources are ready in advance
The interpreter catches the exception, runs the block, and re-raises it afterwards
Only when `__exit__` returns `True`
questions.explanation: `with` desugars to `__enter__`, a `try`, and a `finally` that calls `__exit__` with the exception info. A falsy return from `__exit__` lets the exception propagate; a truthy one swallows it. That suppression is the only way a `with` block hides an error, and returning `True` from `__exit__` to "handle everything" is a well-worn way to swallow a bug and debug it three hours later.

questions.prompt: A module inside a package `app` does `import data`, and there is both a top-level `data.py` and an `app/data.py`. Which one is imported?
options: `app/data.py`, because a packageÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s own directory is searched first
Neither Ã¢â‚¬â€ Python 3 raises `ImportError` for an ambiguous module name
The top-level `data.py`, because Python 3 resolves imports absolutely; you need `from . import data` for the sibling
Whichever was imported first, decided once and then cached in `sys.modules` forever
questions.explanation: Python 3 dropped implicit relative imports. Inside a package, a plain `import data` looks in the top-level namespace, not in the package directory, so the sibling requires the explicit relative form `from . import data`. The related trap is still live: the *scriptÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s* directory is `sys.path[0]`, so a local `json.py` or `random.py` in your project really does shadow the standard library for that run.

questions.prompt: Why is `assert result == [3, 1, 2]` a weak test for a function that returns a list of ids?
options: `==` on lists compares identity rather than contents, so the comparison is meaningless
It pins the ordering into the contract, so a correct reordering fails a correct implementation Ã¢â‚¬â€ assert on a set, a length, or membership instead
`assert` cannot be used with lists at all
pytest rewrites `assert` into a form that only records the failure
questions.explanation: Assert the requirement, not one particular arrangement of it. If order matters, say so in a named constant and sort both sides; if it does not, assert on `set(result)`, on `len(result)`, or on membership. Separately worth knowing: `python -O` strips every `assert` from the bytecode, so assertions are for tests and internal invariants, never for validating user input in production.

questions.prompt: When does the single JSON file stop being the right storage choice for the tracker?
options: As soon as the file passes about 100 KB
Never Ã¢â‚¬â€ JSON files scale indefinitely
When the program is installed as a package rather than run from a checkout
When you need concurrent writers, partial updates, queries across the whole dataset, or transactional guarantees
questions.explanation: The honest limit of a single JSON document is not size but access pattern. Whole-file read-and-write is O(n) per operation, which is fine for hundreds of tasks and wrong for tens of thousands, and it gives you no concurrency and no atomicity unless you build them. The migration path is a repository interface with two implementations Ã¢â‚¬â€ which is only possible if the CLI never touches JSON directly, which is exactly why that boundary exists in the capstone.

questions.prompt: The tracker is asked to finish task 99, which does not exist. What should the process do?
options: Print `no task with id 99` to stderr and exit non-zero, using the code `argparse` already uses for bad input
Print the message to stdout and exit 0, because the program itself ran successfully
Let the failure propagate as an uncaught exception so the traceback is visible
Print the message to stderr and exit 0, because no data was harmed
questions.explanation: Exit code 0 means success and anything else means failure, and both a shell and every CI system key on that distinction. `argparse` already reserves 2 for bad input, so using it for "no such task" is consistent, and stderr keeps diagnostics out of a pipeline consuming stdout. An uncaught traceback is a bug report about your program, not an answer to the userÃ¢â‚¬â„¢s question.

questions.prompt: Why does `save()` write to `tasks.json.tmp` and then `Path.replace()` it over the real file?
options: It is faster, because a small file is written from the page cache
`json.dump` can only write to a file that does not already exist
The rename is atomic on POSIX and on Windows, so the data file is always either the old version or the new one, never half of each
It avoids holding the whole document in memory while writing
questions.explanation: This is the write-temp-then-rename pattern, and it is the difference between losing one command and losing the entire store. `Path.replace` maps to the atomic rename syscall on POSIX and to a replace-semantics `MoveFileEx` on Windows, so the target path is swapped in one step. Opening the real file for writing in place would leave a truncated file if the process died, filled the disk, or lost power mid-write.

courses.title: Advanced Data Structures: Choosing Well Under Real Constraints
courses.subtitle: Hashing, trees, heaps and graphs Ã¢â‚¬â€ built, benchmarked, and chosen with a procedure you can defend
courses.description:
Most data-structure teaching stops at "a hash map is O(1), a tree is O(log n)" and leaves you to guess which one your problem needs. This course is about the second half: the part where the constraints decide, the constant factors show up in a profile, and you have to defend the choice.

Every structure here is implemented from scratch in TypeScript Ã¢â‚¬â€ the hash table with resizing, the red-black tree with all three fix-up cases, the array-backed binary heap, BFS and Dijkstra Ã¢â‚¬â€ and then measured rather than asserted about. The questions are the ones that actually come up: why adversarial hash collisions are a denial-of-service vector, when a binary search loses to a linear scan on cache behaviour, and when an adjacency matrix is genuinely the right answer.

It is a paid course because it assumes you can already program and already have the C course's grounding in pointers and memory. If you are not comfortable reading a loop that walks a linked structure, start with C Programming first.
outcomes: State what a big-O bound does and does not claim, including constants, tightness and space
Explain why a hash table is O(1) in expectation and what an attacker can do about that
Implement and explain every case of the red-black tree fix-up after an insert
Build a binary heap in O(n) and use it to solve top-k problems in O(n log k) without sorting
Choose between an adjacency list and an adjacency matrix from the graph's density
Work through the five constraint questions before choosing a structure, and write down what would change your mind
courses.about_course:
This course exists because the gap in most data-structure curricula is not knowledge, it is judgement. Anyone can be told that a balanced binary search tree gives O(log n) lookup. Far fewer people can answer the question that actually comes up in a code review: why is this a tree and not a sorted array, and what would have to change for that answer to flip?

The material is built around implementations rather than definitions. You will write a hash table that resizes and rehashes, a red-black tree with the full three-case fix-up, a binary heap on a flat array, and BFS and Dijkstra without a library. Writing them is the point. A structure you have implemented is one you can reason about when it misbehaves; a structure you have only read about is one you look up.

The second thread is measurement. Complexity classes are treated honestly throughout Ã¢â‚¬â€ as statements about growth, not about speed. Several lessons are specifically about the cases where the better complexity loses: a linear scan beating binary search on cache behaviour, an O(1)-expected hash table failing under adversarial keys, a sort's crossover point where insertion sort wins. These are not footnotes. They are the difference between a structure that works on a benchmark and one that works in production.

What you are explicitly not getting: a catalogue of every structure that exists, and interview puzzle patterns. Coverage is three modules, and it is meant to be complete rather than padded Ã¢â‚¬â€ you should finish able to defend a choice, not able to recite a table of bounds.
prerequisites: C Programming on TieEdu, or equivalent fluency with pointers and manual memory
Comfort reading and writing recursive functions
Working knowledge of arrays, loops and basic complexity notation
A language runtime for the examples Ã¢â‚¬â€ the course uses TypeScript
audience: Second- and third-year students preparing for systems or backend interviews
Working engineers choosing a data structure for a real workload
Anyone who has memorised complexity tables and wants to know when they apply

modules.title: Module 1 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Complexity, and reading it honestly
modules.summary: Big-O as a statement about growth, the operations that dominate real programs, and the costs that Big-O hides.

lessons.title: What Big-O actually claims
lessons.summary: The definition, stated precisely, and the three things it deliberately does not tell you.

payload.text:
## The claim Big-O makes

Big-O notation is a statement about **how a cost grows as the input grows**, and nothing else. Formally, a function `f(n)` is O(g(n)) if there is some constant `c` and some `nÃ¢â€šâ‚¬` such that for all `n > nÃ¢â€šâ‚¬`, `f(n) Ã¢â€°Â¤ cÃ‚Â·g(n)`.

Read that definition carefully, because three things fall out of it that people routinely get wrong.

**Constants are absorbed.** O(3n) and O(n) are the same class. This is why an algorithm with a lower big-O can still lose a benchmark at small n Ã¢â‚¬â€ and why "but it's only a factor of two" is not an argument against an O(n log n) sort.

**The bound is not tight.** O(nÃ‚Â²) is also O(nÃ‚Â³) and O(2Ã¢ÂÂ¿). Big-O names a ceiling, not the actual cost. When you need the actual cost, the notation is `ÃŽËœ` (theta), which bounds from both sides.

**It says nothing about constants, allocation, or memory.** Big-O is time. Space complexity is a separate claim. A linear-time algorithm that allocates a gigabyte per call can lose to a quadratic one that allocates nothing.
### A useful test: if you cannot state what n is for a given function, you do not yet have an algorithm, you have code.

payload.title: Growth, roughly, for n = 1,000,000
rows: Comparison sort Ã¢â‚¬â€ the practical ceiling

payload.title: Why the crossover is where it is
payload.text: Insertion sort is O(nÃ‚Â²) and beats every library sort below roughly n = 20, because its inner loop is a compare and a shift on data already in cache. Timsort exploits the same fact. "Worse complexity" is not "always slower".

payload.title: The most common misuse
payload.text: Dropping a term because it "does not matter asymptotically" while ignoring that it runs on every request. If the constant is 10Ã‚Â¹Ã‚Â² you have a real problem regardless of the notation.

questions.prompt: What does O(n log n) tell you about an algorithm?
options: Its cost grows no faster than n log n
Its cost is exactly n log n
It uses n log n bytes of memory
It runs in n log n operations on every input size
questions.explanation: Big-O is an upper bound only, so "no faster than" is the accurate reading. The other options either overstate it (exactly) or switch to a different claim (memory, every input).

questions.prompt: An algorithm is O(n) but takes 40 seconds on 10 million items. Is that a contradiction?
options: Yes, O(n) must be fast in absolute terms
No Ã¢â‚¬â€ Big-O hides the constant, and a huge constant can still dominate
No Ã¢â‚¬â€ it is probably O(n log n) in disguise
Yes Ã¢â‚¬â€ 10 million items should be under one second
questions.explanation: The constant factor is entirely outside the notation. This is exactly the case where "but asymptotically better" does not rescue the code.

questions.prompt: Why is a hash map lookup usually quoted as O(1) even though it is really O(n) in the worst case?
options: Because the worst case cannot happen in practice
Because O(1) is the average case and we state that separately
Because hashing is a constant-time operation
Because the table is resized to stay full
questions.explanation: It is an expected/average-case bound. Saying "O(1)" unqualified hides that an adversarial key set can degrade it Ã¢â‚¬â€ the reason adversarial-hash DoS is a real vulnerability.

lessons.title: The operations that actually dominate
lessons.summary: Counting, not guessing: instrument a real workload and find the hot operations before optimising anything.

payload.text:
## Optimise the thing you measured

The instinct to improve an algorithm before measuring is the single most common way to waste a week. In most real services, a surprising fraction of time is spent somewhere that has nothing to do with the algorithm anyone is worried about.

In a typical request-serving service, the rough split is:

- **Network and serialisation** Ã¢â‚¬â€ often the largest single cost, and invisible in profiles that only look at CPU.
- **Database round-trips** Ã¢â‚¬â€ a query plan matters more than your loop.
- **Allocation and garbage collection** Ã¢â‚¬â€ proportional to bytes touched, not to algorithmic elegance.
- **The actual algorithm** Ã¢â‚¬â€ frequently a small slice of the total.

The corollary is uncomfortable: making an O(nÃ‚Â²) call into an O(n log n) call on a function that consumed 2% of the request time improves the request by well under 2%.
### Measure first, then decide. The complexity class tells you the ceiling on your win; the profiler tells you the size of it.

payload.title: Amortised cost is the number to reason with
payload.text: A dynamic array that occasionally doubles has an O(n) worst-case push but O(1) amortised. Hash resizing and repeated string concatenation in a loop are the same shape. Judge data structures by amortised cost over a run, not by a single worst case.

payload.title: Cache and asymptotics are different axes
payload.text: An O(n) pass over a 200 MB array with sequential access can beat an O(log n) binary search over the same data, because each cache miss costs more than a hundred arithmetic operations. Both facts are true; which one wins is a measurement question.

modules.title: Module 2 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Structures that hold data under pressure
modules.summary: Hashing, trees, heaps and the trade-offs between them, built and benchmarked rather than defined.

lessons.title: Hashing, and why the worst case is a security problem
lessons.summary: Buckets, collisions, load factor, and the deliberate-collision denial of service.

payload.text:
## How a hash table actually works

A hash table is an array of buckets. A key is run through a hash function to get an index; the entry goes in that bucket. Lookup repeats the process and scans the bucket for a key match.

That is the whole idea, and every property of the structure follows from two numbers: the **load factor** (entries ÃƒÂ· buckets) and the **average bucket length** (itself a function of load factor and how good the hash is).

**Resizing.** When the load factor crosses a threshold, the table doubles and every entry is rehashed. Doubling rather than growing by a fixed amount is what keeps the *amortised* cost of an insert O(1): each entry is moved O(log n) times over its lifetime, so the average cost per insert is constant.

**Collisions are not exceptional.** With a decent hash and a reasonable load factor, some buckets hold two entries all the time. Open addressing (probe forward) and chaining (linked list per bucket) are the two standard resolutions, and the choice trades cache locality against memory overhead.
### Hashing gives you O(1) *expected* behaviour, not guaranteed. The gap between those two words is where a denial-of-service bug lives.

payload.title: Adversarial collisions are a denial-of-service vector
payload.text: If an attacker can submit keys, they can search for keys that all land in one bucket. A table that was O(1) becomes O(n) per operation, and enough of them becomes a CPU-exhaustion attack. This is why some runtimes randomise the hash seed per process: it does not make collisions impossible, it makes them un-targetable by the attacker.

payload.title: Hash maps do not preserve order
payload.text: If you find yourself sorting a `Map`'s keys on every request, you have built an ordered structure with an O(n log n) tax on every operation. Either keep a sorted array alongside, or use a tree.

questions.prompt: Why does a hash table grow by doubling rather than by 10%?
options: Doubling uses less memory
Doubling keeps the amortised cost of each insert O(1), because each entry is rehashed only O(log n) times
A 10% growth factor reduces collisions more effectively
It is only faster to rehash in practice, the theory is the same
questions.explanation: With 10% growth, an entry is rehashed O(n) times over its life, so the total cost of n inserts is O(nÃ‚Â²) and there is no amortised guarantee. Doubling is what makes the bound hold.

questions.prompt: A service accepts user-supplied keys and a hash map has slowed to a crawl. What is the most likely cause?
options: The load factor is too low
The hash function is colliding for the supplied keys, so buckets are long
The table needs to be shrunk
Reshashing happens too often
questions.explanation: Attacker-chosen keys that collide defeat the expected O(1). This is the classic algorithmic-complexity DoS, and the fix is a seeded or randomised hash.

questions.prompt: What does the load factor of 0.75 with chaining actually tell you?
options: 75% of lookups are cache misses
On average 0.75 entries per bucket, which is the target the table resizes to maintain
The table will resize again after 75% more inserts
Memory usage is 75% of the bucket array
questions.explanation: Load factor is entries per bucket, so 0.75 means the average bucket holds about 0.75 entries. The table grows to keep it there, which bounds expected bucket length and therefore expected lookup cost.

lessons.title: Trees: when order is the requirement
lessons.summary: Binary search trees, the balance invariant, and what self-balancing actually buys you.

payload.text:
## The problem trees solve

A hash map gives O(1) expected but no ordering. Sometimes ordering *is* the requirement:

- "the 10 cheapest orders in this range" Ã¢â‚¬â€ needs order, not membership.
- "everything between 12:00 and 14:00" Ã¢â‚¬â€ a range query.
- "next available slot" Ã¢â‚¬â€ ordered search, not equality.

A binary search tree stores keys so that an in-order traversal yields them sorted. The search cost is O(height), which is the whole story: a balanced tree has height O(log n) and gives O(log n) search; a degenerate tree has height O(n) and gives back the linear scan you were trying to avoid.
### A BST without a balance invariant is a liability. Inserting sorted data into a naive BST produces a linked list with extra pointer dereferences.

payload.title: Structure comparison
B+ trees are why your database is fast
payload.text: Disk pages hold hundreds of keys, so a B+ tree of fanout 500 has height 3 for billions of rows. That is why "sequential index access" beats a hash lookup for range queries in every real RDBMS.

questions.prompt: You insert keys 1..1,000,000 in ascending order into a naive BST. What is the resulting lookup cost?
options: O(log n) Ã¢â‚¬â€ insertion order does not matter
O(n) Ã¢â‚¬â€ the tree degenerates into a linked list
O(n log n)
O(1) Ã¢â‚¬â€ the tree self-balances
questions.explanation: A naive BST with sorted input puts every new node as the rightmost child, giving height n. This is exactly the failure that balance invariants exist to prevent.

questions.prompt: Which query is the hash map structurally unable to answer efficiently?
options: Does this exact key exist?
How many distinct keys are there?
List all keys between "m" and "p" in order
Is this value already in the set?
questions.explanation: Hash maps expose no order, so a range query degrades to scanning every bucket and sorting the survivors Ã¢â‚¬â€ O(n) plus O(n log n).

questions.prompt: What invariant does the red-black colour property maintain?
options: That keys are stored in sorted order in memory
That no two adjacent nodes are red, keeping every root-to-leaf path within a factor of two of every other
That the tree never needs to rotate
That every leaf is at the same depth
questions.explanation: Equal black-heights on all root-to-leaf paths are what bound the height to 2Ã‚Â·logÃ¢â€šâ€š(n+1). Adjacent reds are what make the fix-up cases tractable.

lessons.title: Heaps, priority queues and top-k without sorting
lessons.summary: The binary heap invariant, sift-up/sift-down, and the O(n log k) trick for top-k problems.

payload.text:
## The heap invariant

A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in a flat array, where every parent is at least as large as (max-heap) or at most as large as (min-heap) each of its children. The key property is what you get *without* the tree being sorted: the root is always the extreme element, in O(1).

That is all a priority queue needs, and it is why heaps beat balanced trees for this job: no pointers, no rebalancing, excellent cache behaviour, and insertion is O(log n) amortised with a very small constant.
### For "what is the largest / next / most urgent thing", a heap is the right structure. Reach for a tree only when you also need ordered traversal.

payload.title: Build a heap in O(n), not O(n log n)
payload.text: Pushing n elements one at a time is O(n log n). Calling siftDown from the last internal node down to the root is O(n), because most nodes are near the leaves and barely sift. `new MinHeap(arr)` should do the latter.

payload.title: Heaps are not sorted and cannot be traversed in order
payload.text: Reading the underlying array left to right gives the level-order layout, which is meaningless as a sort. If you need sorted output, pop everything (O(n log n)) or use a different structure.

questions.prompt: Finding the top 10 of 1,000,000 items. What is the best approach?
options: Sort all 1,000,000 and take the first 10 Ã¢â‚¬â€ O(n log n)
Keep a max-heap of size 10 while streaming Ã¢â‚¬â€ O(n log 10)
Sort only the first 100 items and hope
Binary search the range of values
questions.explanation: Bounded memory and O(n log k) time. A full sort does strictly more work and needs O(n) memory, for the same answer.

questions.prompt: In a max-heap, where does the largest element live?
options: Anywhere in the last level
At a leaf, since leaves are added last
At the root, index 0
Whichever leaf was inserted last
questions.explanation: The heap invariant only constrains parent-vs-child, so the maximum must be a root (a node with no parent to dominate it). Everything else in the heap is unordered.

questions.prompt: Building a heap by inserting n elements one at a time costs O(n log n). Why is bottom-up construction O(n)?
options: It performs fewer comparisons per element
Most nodes near the leaves sift only a short distance, and the total work sums to O(n)
It uses a different, cheaper algorithm
It skips the sift step entirely
questions.explanation: Sum over all nodes of sift distance. The deepest nodes are numerous but barely move; the few near the root sift far. The series converges to O(n).

modules.title: Module 3 Ã¢â‚¬â€ Choosing, and knowing when you are done
modules.summary: Graph structures, space/time trade-offs, and a defensible decision procedure for picking a structure under real constraints.

lessons.title: Graphs: adjacency lists beat matrices, and when the matrix wins
lessons.summary: Representation, traversal, and the cases where the denser structure is genuinely correct.

payload.text:
## How to store a graph

A graph is nodes and edges. Two representations dominate:

**Adjacency list** Ã¢â‚¬â€ for each node, the list of its neighbours. Space is O(V + E). Traversal of all neighbours is proportional to the actual degree.

**Adjacency matrix** Ã¢â‚¬â€ a VÃƒâ€”V table of booleans or weights. Space is O(VÃ‚Â²). Membership of a specific edge is O(1).

The crossover is density. For a sparse graph the list is dramatically smaller; for a dense graph the matrix's constant factor and cache layout can win despite the quadratic space. Most real graphs are sparse Ã¢â‚¬â€ social, road, dependency and reference graphs are all far below the E Ã¢â€°Ë† VÃ‚Â² threshold Ã¢â‚¬â€ so the list is the default and the matrix is the special case.
### Rule of thumb: adjacency list unless you need O(1) edge-membership queries in a dense graph, or you intend to run an algorithm that benefits from random edge access.

payload.title: Dijkstra requires non-negative weights
payload.text: A single negative edge breaks the "finalised node" assumption, and the algorithm silently returns wrong distances. With negative edges you need Bellman-Ford (O(VÃ‚Â·E)), and with negative *cycles* the problem is unbounded Ã¢â‚¬â€ no algorithm can answer it.

payload.title: Graph structure choices
rows: O(V Ã‚Â· E), detects negative cycles

questions.prompt: Why is `queue.shift()` a poor choice inside BFS?
options: It does not preserve FIFO order
It is O(n) per call, making the traversal O(nÃ‚Â·V) overall
It cannot hold numbers
It reallocates on every call
questions.explanation: FIFO order is correct, but shift() must reindex the whole array each time. An index-based ring buffer or a linked queue gives amortised O(1).

questions.prompt: Dijkstra is run on a graph containing one edge of weight -5. What happens?
options: It returns correct distances, just more slowly
It silently returns incorrect distances, because a finalised node may later be improved
It throws an error
It degrades gracefully to Bellman-Ford
questions.explanation: The correctness argument assumes weights are non-negative. With a negative edge, a node marked final can still be improved Ã¢â‚¬â€ the failure is wrong output, not a crash, which is the dangerous part.

questions.prompt: A graph has 1,000,000 nodes and 4,000,000 edges, and you need to know which components it has. Best structure?
options: Adjacency matrix Ã¢â‚¬â€ 10Ã‚Â¹Ã‚Â² booleans, but constant-time queries
Adjacency list plus Union-Find
A binary heap over all nodes
A BFS from every node in turn
questions.explanation: Connectivity is exactly what Union-Find is for, at O(EÃ‚Â·ÃŽÂ±(V)) with no traversal. A matrix here would need 10Ã‚Â¹Ã‚Â² cells, and BFS from every node is O(VÃ‚Â·(V+E)).

lessons.title: A decision procedure you can defend in a review
lessons.summary: Constraints first, structure second: the questions to ask before choosing anything.

payload.text:
## Ask the constraints before naming a structure

Most bad data-structure choices are not wrong answers to an unasked question. They are reasonable answers to a question nobody asked. Before opening an editor, write down:

**1. What are the actual operations, with frequencies?**
A structure chosen for the wrong operation is wrong regardless of its asymptotics. A config read once at boot and a ledger appended 10,000 times per second have opposite requirements.

**2. What are the access patterns, not just the accesses?**
Membership? Range? Top-k? Ordered traversal? Nearest neighbour? Prefix search? These map to different structures, and no single structure is best at all of them.

**3. What is the data lifetime and size?**
Fits in cache? Larger than RAM? Grows without bound? This single fact decides between in-memory and on-disk structures more often than any other.

**4. What are the update semantics?**
Mostly immutable after build? Frequent inserts? Frequent deletes in the middle? Each rules structures in or out.

**5. What is the concurrency requirement?**
Single-threaded, lock-based, or lock-free? Many "obvious" structures have no safe concurrent story, and retrofitting one later is a rewrite.
### Write these five answers down before choosing. If you cannot fill them in, the design is not ready, and no amount of structure-hopping will fix that.

payload.title: Worked example: session store, 50k active sessions, 2k reads/s per node
rows: Lookup by opaque id, delete on expiry
Fits in memory; entries expire on a timer
In-memory, no persistence layer in the hot path
Tombstones plus periodic sweep, not in-order delete
Multiple node processes, partitioned by hash
No shared mutable state; per-partition ownership

payload.title: Complexity is a tie-breaker, not a starting point
payload.text: Once the five constraints point at one or two candidates, that is when big-O decides. Using big-O first tends to pick a theoretically superior structure that cannot satisfy constraint 3.

payload.title: Write down what would make you change your mind
payload.text: "We will revisit this if p99 exceeds 50 ms" or "if the working set stops fitting in cache". A structure chosen without a trigger condition will be defended long after it stopped being right.

study_plan_phases.title: Set Your Baseline & Frame Your Story
study_plan_phases.summary: Decide what you are actually being interviewed for, then build the narrative that carries you through every round.

payload.text:
### Start here

Most candidates lose rounds in the first ten minutes because they never decided what story they are telling. Write it down before you write any code.

1. **Name the exact role.** "Backend SDE-1 at a product company" and "Full-stack SDE-1 at a product company" have different interview weights. Pick one line and stay on it.
2. **List your three strongest projects.** For each, be able to answer: what problem, why that design, what you personally built, what you would change today.
3. **Write your one-line pitch.** Thirty seconds, no jargon, no "passionate about". Example: *"I build backend systems that keep financial data consistent under load, most recently at a payments company."*
4. **Set your time budget.** Divide the remaining days across phases. A plan you finish beats a plan you abandon on day five.

payload.title: Day 1-2 deliverables
items: Target role and company written on one line
Resume trimmed to one page, no role-specific formatting hacks
Three project deep-dives written in the problem Ã¢â€ â€™ design Ã¢â€ â€™ build Ã¢â€ â€™ improve shape
Thirty-second pitch recorded on your phone, played back twice
Realistic day budget agreed with yourself
Two questions written for the interviewer (never walk in with none)

payload.title: Why this phase is first
payload.text: Interviewers form an early hypothesis about your level. A crisp, specific story in the opening minutes raises the bar for the rest of the round, and it makes the hard questions easier to answer honestly.

study_plan_phases.title: Data Structures & Algorithms
study_plan_phases.summary: The largest single block of marks in most loops. Master the patterns, not the problem list.

payload.text:
### Learn patterns, not problems

Interviews reuse roughly a dozen patterns with new wrappers. If you can recognise the pattern in the first ninety seconds, you are already ahead of most candidates who memorised 300 solutions.

- **Core linear structures** Ã¢â‚¬â€ arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, deques. Two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums.
- **Non-linear** Ã¢â‚¬â€ hash maps, heaps, balanced trees, tries, disjoint-set union.
- **Graphs** Ã¢â‚¬â€ BFS/DFS, topological sort, connected components, shortest path, union-find.
- **Advanced** Ã¢â‚¬â€ binary search on answer, backtracking, greedy with proof, DP on trees and intervals.

For every problem, say the complexity out loud **before** you write code, then state the space cost. Interviewers grade your reasoning as much as the result.

payload.title: Complexity cheat sheet
Practice gate Ã¢â‚¬â€ do not skip ahead until this passes
items: Two pointers and sliding window: 6 problems solved from scratch
Heap problems: able to explain when a min-heap beats sorting
BFS and DFS: can state when each is the right tool before coding
Binary search on answer: practised at least twice
Backtracking: template internalised, including pruning
Every problem: complexity stated aloud first, edge cases named
At least one timed set of 3 problems in 75 minutes

payload.title: Where to practise

links.label: LeetCode Ã¢â‚¬â€ problem list, filter by pattern
NeetCode roadmap Ã¢â‚¬â€ curated pattern ordering
CP-Algorithms Ã¢â‚¬â€ reference explanations
Big-O cheat sheet

study_plan_phases.title: Computer Science Fundamentals
study_plan_phases.summary: Operating systems, networking and databases Ã¢â‚¬â€ the questions that separate a mid-level hire from a senior one.

payload.text:
### Operating systems

- Process vs thread, and why context switching costs you throughput
- Race conditions, mutexes vs semaphores, and deadlock conditions
- Paging, virtual memory, page faults, and what a page fault really costs
- I/O models: blocking, non-blocking, async/await, and when each is correct

### Networking

- What happens between typing a URL and the first byte of the response
- TCP vs UDP, three-way handshake, and reliability trade-offs
- HTTP status classes, keep-alive, TLS handshake, and proxies
- Idempotency, retries with backoff, rate limiting, and load balancing

### Databases

- Indexes: B-tree structure, composite index column order, covering indexes
- Normalisation vs denormalisation, and the read/write trade-off
- ACID, isolation levels, and what a non-repeatable read means in practice
- Connection pooling, N+1 queries, and pagination strategies

payload.title: How to answer a fundamentals question you have forgotten
payload.text: Say what you remember, name the trade-off you are sure about, and say plainly that you would look it up. "I do not remember the exact page size, but it is chosen to match disk block size so one disk read maps to one page" is a strong answer. Bluffing a number is not.

payload.title: Fundamentals self-test
items: Can explain the full URL-to-response path in under three minutes
Can describe deadlock and give a real prevention strategy
Can state all four ACID properties with an example failure each
Can explain why a composite index on (a, b) does not help queries filtering on b alone
Can describe what happens when a query plan ignores your index

study_plan_phases.title: System Design Fundamentals
study_plan_phases.summary: Start from requirements, not from Kafka. A structured, honest design beats a fashionable stack.

payload.text:
### The four-step frame

1. **Clarify requirements.** Functional, non-functional, and the actual scale. Estimate users, requests per second, and read/write ratio out loud before drawing anything.
2. **Estimate the numbers.** Daily active users, peak multiplier, storage per entity, bandwidth. Rough arithmetic is fine Ã¢â‚¬â€ showing the method is the point.
3. **Design the high-level shape.** API surface, main services, storage choice, and the data flow. Then go deep on exactly one component, usually the one the interviewer picks.
4. **Discuss the trade-offs.** Caching, sharding, replication, queues, consistency model, and what breaks first under ten times the load.

Red flags in a design round: jumping to a specific technology before requirements are agreed, ignoring failure modes, and designing for a scale nobody asked for.

payload.title: Common building blocks and when to reach for them
rows: Need to absorb bursts or decouple services
Reads dominate and can be slightly stale
Single-node storage or write throughput is the ceiling
Static or cacheable content, global users
Any retried write, payments, order creation

payload.title: Before you finish any design round
items: Requirements and scale stated out loud at the start
Numbers estimated, not guessed
Exactly one component taken deep rather than five taken shallow
Data model stated with the access patterns it supports
One failure scenario walked end to end
Metrics named: what you would alert on in production

study_plan_phases.title: Project Deep-Dive & Behavioural
study_plan_phases.summary: The round where most technically strong candidates lose. Prepare specifics, not adjectives.

payload.text:
### Answering "tell me about a project"

Use a fixed 90-second structure and reuse it every time:

- **Context (15s)** Ã¢â‚¬â€ what the product did and why it existed
- **Your role (15s)** Ã¢â‚¬â€ the part you personally owned, stated plainly
- **The hard part (30s)** Ã¢â‚¬â€ the trade-off you made and the alternative you rejected
- **The outcome (20s)** Ã¢â‚¬â€ a number, a latency improvement, a defect class removed
- **The reflection (10s)** Ã¢â‚¬â€ what you would redo, which reads as senior

Never describe a team as "we" for the work you did, and never claim ownership of a decision you cannot defend under follow-up questions.

payload.title: STAR stories to have ready
items: Conflict with a teammate, and how you resolved it without escalation
A deadline you missed, and what you did about it
The best technical decision you made that a reviewer initially disagreed with
A production incident you were involved in
Receiving harsh feedback, and what changed afterwards
A time you said no to a scope increase, and how you handled it

payload.title: If you do not have a real example
payload.text: Say so and pivot to a hypothetical: "I have not handled that exact situation, but here is how I would approach it." Interviewers accept this far more often than a stretched story that collapses on the second question.

study_plan_phases.title: Mock Drives & Final Review
study_plan_phases.summary: Simulate the real loop under real time pressure, then fix what the mocks actually exposed.

payload.text:
### Rehearse the whole loop, not just the questions

- **Full mock drives.** 45 minutes, one algorithm problem, one project deep-dive, one design question, and behavioural questions at the end. Do it on a call, out loud, with someone watching.
- **Explain while you code.** Narrate your reasoning continuously. Silent coding is read as guessing.
- **Log every mock.** Write down what you fumbled, not what you answered well. Patterns repeat across mocks.
- **Close the loop.** Re-solve every problem you could not finish within the time limit, without a timer this time.

payload.title: Final gate Ã¢â‚¬â€ the week of the interview
items: Two full mock drives completed with a human
Weakest three topics re-studied and re-tested cold
Resume, pitch and three project stories rehearsed aloud
Company research done honestly: products, public engineering blog, recent news
Questions for the interviewer written down
Logistics confirmed: link, time zone, camera, backup phone charged

payload.title: On company-specific preparation
payload.text: This plan covers standard engineering interview preparation. Company-specific process details change often and are not verified here Ã¢â‚¬â€ check the company page on this site and confirm anything time-sensitive with your recruiter before relying on it.

questions.question: Which keyword is used to inherit a class in Java?
questions.explanation: The extends keyword is used for class inheritance in Java.

questions.question: What is the entry point of a Java program?
questions.explanation: public static void main(String[] args) is the entry point.

questions.question: Java is a platform-independent language.
questions.explanation: Java compiles to bytecode which runs on any JVM, making it platform-independent.

questions.question: Which is NOT a primitive type in Java?
questions.explanation: String is a class (object type), not a primitive.

questions.question: What is the default value of an uninitialized int variable?
questions.explanation: Instance int fields default to 0. Local int variables must be initialized before use.

questions.question: Which of the following are OOP principles?
questions.explanation: Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism, and Abstraction are the four OOP principles.

questions.question: Which keyword prevents a method from being overridden?
questions.explanation: The final keyword prevents overriding of methods and inheritance of classes.

questions.question: What is the parent class of all Java classes?
questions.explanation: java.lang.Object is the root of the class hierarchy.

questions.question: Which statements are true about abstract classes?
questions.explanation: Abstract classes can have constructors, abstract and concrete methods, but cannot be instantiated directly.

questions.question: Which access modifier provides the most restrictive access?
questions.explanation: private is the most restrictive Ã¢â‚¬â€ only accessible within the same class.

questions.question: Which collection class allows duplicate elements?
questions.explanation: ArrayList allows duplicate elements; HashSet and TreeSet do not.

questions.question: What data structure does HashMap internally use?

options.text: Hash Table with Linked List/Binary Tree

questions.explanation: HashMap uses buckets (array) with linked lists (or trees for large buckets) for collision handling.

questions.question: Which interface does HashMap implement?
questions.explanation: HashMap implements the Map interface.

questions.question: Which collection types maintain insertion order?
questions.explanation: ArrayList and LinkedHashMap maintain insertion order. TreeMap sorts by key, HashSet has no order.

questions.question: ArrayList is thread-safe by default.
questions.explanation: ArrayList is NOT thread-safe. Use Collections.synchronizedList() or CopyOnWriteArrayList for thread safety.

questions.question: Which block is used to handle exceptions?
questions.explanation: try-catch blocks handle exceptions in Java.

questions.question: Which are checked exceptions?
questions.explanation: IOException and SQLException are checked exceptions. RuntimeException subclasses are unchecked.

questions.question: What does the finally block do?
questions.explanation: finally always executes after try-catch, regardless of whether an exception occurred.

questions.question: A method can throw multiple checked exceptions using multiple throws clauses.
questions.explanation: A throws clause can list multiple exceptions separated by commas: throws IOException, SQLException.

questions.question: Which class is the root of all unchecked exceptions?
questions.explanation: RuntimeException is the root of all unchecked exceptions.

questions.question: Which class is used to create a thread by subclassing?
questions.explanation: Extend the Thread class or implement Runnable. Thread is the class used for subclassing.

questions.question: Which methods are used for thread synchronization?
questions.explanation: synchronized, volatile, and wait() are used for synchronization. yield() is a hint to the scheduler.

questions.question: Java supports multiple inheritance of classes.
questions.explanation: Java does not support multiple inheritance of classes to avoid the diamond problem. Use interfaces instead.

questions.question: What does the wait() method do?

options.text: Releases the lock and waits for notify()

questions.explanation: wait() releases the object lock and waits until notify() or notifyAll() is called.

questions.question: Which interface should you implement for a thread that returns a result?
questions.explanation: Callable.call() can return a value and throw checked exceptions.

questions.question: What does JVM stand for?
questions.explanation: JVM = Java Virtual Machine, which executes Java bytecode.

questions.question: Where does garbage collection occur?
questions.explanation: Garbage collection operates on the heap memory where objects are allocated.

questions.question: What is JIT compilation?
questions.explanation: JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler compiles frequently executed methods to native code at runtime.

questions.question: Which memory areas are managed by the JVM?
questions.explanation: JVM manages Heap, Stack, and Method Area. Registers are managed by the underlying CPU.

questions.question: System.gc() guarantees immediate garbage collection.
questions.explanation: System.gc() is a suggestion only; the JVM may ignore it. No guarantee of immediate collection.

questions.question: Which Java version introduced the var keyword for local variable type inference?
questions.explanation: Java 10 introduced var for local variable type inference.

questions.question: Which are features introduced in Java 8?
questions.explanation: Java 8 introduced lambdas, streams, and default methods. Records came in Java 14/16.

questions.question: What does the Optional class help avoid?
questions.explanation: Optional helps avoid NullPointerException by providing a container for possibly-null values.

questions.question: Which functional interface has the method apply()?
questions.explanation: Function<T,R> has apply(). Predicate has test(), Consumer has accept(), Supplier has get().

questions.question: A Java interface can have default methods with implementations (Java 8+).
questions.explanation: Java 8 introduced default methods allowing interfaces to have method implementations.

questions.question: Which symbol is used for comments in Python?
questions.explanation: Python uses # for single-line comments.

questions.question: Python is an interpreted language.
questions.explanation: Python source is executed line by line by the interpreter (after bytecode compilation).

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a built-in Python data type?
questions.explanation: array is from the array module; list, tuple and dict are built-in.

questions.question: What is the output of type(3 / 2) in Python 3?
questions.explanation: The / operator always returns a float in Python 3; use // for floor division.

questions.question: Which keyword defines a function in Python?
questions.explanation: Python uses def to define functions.

questions.question: What does *args allow in a function definition?
questions.explanation: *args collects any number of positional arguments into a tuple.

questions.question: Which method is called when an object is instantiated?
questions.explanation: __init__ is the constructor, called when a new instance is created.

questions.question: Which are valid ways to achieve inheritance in Python?

options.text: class Child: pass with Parent assignment

questions.explanation: Python supports class Child(Parent) and multiple inheritance class Child(A, B).

questions.question: Which block handles exceptions in Python?
questions.explanation: Python uses try/except blocks to catch exceptions.

questions.question: Which statement always executes after try/except?
questions.explanation: finally always runs whether or not an exception occurred.

questions.question: Which header provides cout in C++?
questions.explanation: <iostream> declares std::cout.

questions.question: C++ supports function overloading.
questions.explanation: Functions with the same name but different parameter lists can coexist.

questions.question: What does dereferencing a pointer do?

options.text: Returns the value stored at its address

questions.explanation: The * operator accesses the value at the pointed-to address.

questions.question: What is a dangling pointer?

options.text: A pointer to memory that has been freed

questions.explanation: After delete/free the pointer still holds the old address â€” memory is no longer valid.

questions.question: Which access specifier allows access only within the class?
